questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Norepinephrine is produced by
questions.explanation: Norepinephrine is synthesized from dopamine via hydroxylation by dopamine beta-hydroxylase, which requires vitamin C (ascorbic acid) and copper as a cofactor. This is the primary pathway for norepinephrine production in the adrenal medulla and CNS neurons.
questions.keyConcept: Catecholamine synthesis pathway and dopamine beta-hydroxylase reaction

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Production of norepinephrine from dopamine requires
questions.explanation: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase catalyzes the hydroxylation of dopamine to norepinephrine. This enzyme is a copper-containing monooxygenase that requires vitamin C as an electron donor and tetrahydrobiopterin as a cofactor. Both cofactors are essential for activity, hence answer D.
questions.keyConcept: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase cofactors: copper, vitamin C, and tetrahydrobiopterin

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Production of epinephrine from nor-epinephrine requires
questions.explanation: Epinephrine is synthesized from norepinephrine by phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PNMT), which uses S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) as the methyl donor. PNMT is expressed primarily in the adrenal medulla. The combination of PNMT enzyme and SAM availability makes both factors necessary.
questions.keyConcept: PNMT methylates norepinephrine to epinephrine using SAM as methyl donor

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Catecholamines are catabolized by
questions.explanation: Catecholamines are catabolized by both MAO (monoamine oxidase) and COMT (catechol O-methyltransferase), acting sequentially or independently. MAO acts first in mitochondria, followed by aldehyde dehydrogenase; COMT O-methylates catecholamines directly. Both pathways contribute to VMA production.
questions.keyConcept: Dual catabolism of catecholamines by MAO and COMT pathways
options: monoamine oxidase (MAO), followed by aldehyde dehydrogenase.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The end product of adrenaline and noradrenaline catabolism is
questions.explanation: Vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) is the primary urinary metabolite of both epinephrine and norepinephrine. It is formed through combined MAO and COMT action on catecholamines, then further metabolism to VMA. Elevated VMA is a key diagnostic marker for pheochromocytoma.
questions.keyConcept: VMA as the end product of catecholamine catabolism and tumor marker

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: To increase the synthesis of catecholamines in the brain, a patient with Parkinsonism may be given
questions.explanation: L-dopa (levodopa) is the direct precursor of dopamine and is administered to increase catecholamine synthesis in Parkinson's disease, where dopaminergic neurons have degenerated. L-dopa crosses the blood-brain barrier unlike dopamine itself, then is converted to dopamine by DOPA decarboxylase.
questions.keyConcept: L-dopa as dopamine precursor in Parkinson's disease treatment

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Decarboxylation of 5-hydroxytryptophan results in formation of
questions.explanation: 5-hydroxytryptophan is decarboxylated by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (ALAD) to form serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine). This is the second step in serotonin biosynthesis, following hydroxylation of tryptophan by tryptophan hydroxylase.
questions.keyConcept: Serotonin synthesis from 5-hydroxytryptophan via decarboxylation

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Serotonin is
questions.explanation: Serotonin is chemically 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT), synthesized from tryptophan. It is not a tyrosine derivative (that would be catecholamines); rather, it is an indoleamine derived from tryptophan. Melatonin is formed from serotonin by N-acetylation and O-methylation, not the reverse.
questions.keyConcept: Serotonin (5-HT) as an indoleamine, not a catecholamine
options: produced by N-acetylation and O-methylation of melatonin.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Serotonin is catabolized by
questions.explanation: Serotonin is catabolized primarily by monoamine oxidase (MAO), which oxidatively deaminates it to 5-hydroxyindoleacetaldehyde, further converted to 5-HIAA. COMT does not significantly metabolize serotonin since it is not a catecholamine.
questions.keyConcept: MAO as the primary catabolic enzyme for serotonin

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following increases in 24-hour urine with pheochromocytoma (adrenaline-secreting tumor)?
questions.explanation: In pheochromocytoma, excess catecholamines are secreted and metabolized, producing elevated urinary vanillylmandelic acid (VMA). VMA is the end product of both epinephrine and norepinephrine catabolism and is routinely measured as a diagnostic marker for this tumor.
questions.keyConcept: VMA elevation in urine as diagnostic marker for pheochromocytoma

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following may be measured in 24-hour urine to diagnose carcinoid syndrome (argentaffinoma, serotonin-secreting tumor)?
questions.explanation: Carcinoid syndrome (argentaffinoma) secretes serotonin, which is metabolized to 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA). Measuring 24-hour urinary 5-HIAA is the standard diagnostic test for carcinoid syndrome, as it reflects total serotonin turnover.
questions.keyConcept: 5-HIAA as urinary marker for carcinoid syndrome

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following may serve as a tumor marker?
questions.explanation: Both VMA (from catecholamine-secreting tumors like pheochromocytoma) and 5-HIAA (from carcinoid tumors) can serve as tumor markers when measured in 24-hour urine collections. These metabolites provide specific diagnostic clues for neuroendocrine tumors.
questions.keyConcept: VMA and 5-HIAA as neuroendocrine tumor markers

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following enzymes is important for synthesis of both epinephrine and melatonin?
questions.explanation: Aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (ALAD) is required for synthesis of both epinephrine (via DOPA to dopamine pathway) and melatonin (via 5-HTP to serotonin pathway). Dihydrobiopterin reductase is also involved in catecholamine synthesis, making both essential.
questions.keyConcept: ALAD as common enzyme in both catecholamine and melatonin synthesis

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Histamine is formed from histidine by
questions.explanation: Histidine decarboxylase converts histidine to histamine, and this enzyme requires pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) as a cofactor. Aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase also participates in histamine metabolism in some contexts, requiring the same cofactor.
questions.keyConcept: Histamine synthesis from histidine requiring PLP cofactor
options: a reaction that requires pyridoxal phosphate.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Tyramine
questions.explanation: Tyramine is formed by bacterial decarboxylation of tyrosine in aged foods (cheese, wine). It displaces catecholamines from synaptic vesicles, and in patients on MAO inhibitors, this can cause massive catecholamine release leading to hypertensive crisis (the 'cheese effect').
questions.keyConcept: Tyramine in aged foods and cheese effect with MAO inhibitors
options: is the decarboxylation product of tyrosine, which is present in aged food.
can displace catecholamines from their stores.
may precipitate a hypertensive crisis in patients taking MAO inhibitors as anti-depressant.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Nitric oxide is a hormone and a neurotransmitter produced
questions.explanation: Nitric oxide (NO) is synthesized from arginine by nitric oxide synthase (NOS), which requires oxygen and NADPH. Glycine is not a precursor for NO; it is involved in purine metabolism and as a neurotransmitter. The NOS reaction also produces citrulline.
questions.keyConcept: NO synthesis from arginine by NOS requiring O2 and NADPH
options: by the action of nitric oxide synthase.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Nitric oxide synthase
questions.explanation: Nitric oxide synthase exists as three isozymes: neuronal (nNOS), endothelial (eNOS), and phagocytic/inducible (iNOS). All isoforms convert arginine to citrulline and NO using NADPH and oxygen. The reaction produces both citrulline and nitric oxide as products.
questions.keyConcept: Three NOS isoforms: neuronal, endothelial, and phagocytic
options: acts on arginine and needs Oxygen and NADPH.
has three isozymes: neuronal, endothelial and phagocytic.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which nitric oxide synthase isozyme is
questions.explanation: The phagocytic (inducible) nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) is calcium-independent, unlike nNOS and eNOS which require calmodulin and calcium for activity. iNOS is induced by cytokines in macrophages during immune responses and produces large amounts of NO for antimicrobial defense.
questions.keyConcept: iNOS as calcium-independent NOS isozyme in phagocytes

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Urea cycle is a pathway that
questions.explanation: The urea cycle occurs exclusively in the liver (hepatocytes) and is the body's mechanism for converting toxic ammonia (NH3) into urea for excretion. It does not produce ammonia from urea; that would be the reverse reaction which does not occur physiologically.
questions.keyConcept: Urea cycle location in liver and its role in ammonia detoxification
options: takes place mainly in the liver cells.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In the urea cycle, urea is produced from
questions.explanation: Arginine is cleaved by arginase to produce urea and ornithine in the final step of the urea cycle. Fumarate is produced earlier from argininosuccinate. Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase initiates the cycle by fixing ammonia and CO2.
questions.keyConcept: Arginase cleavage of arginine to produce urea and ornithine
options: carbon dioxide and ammonium ions by carbamoyl phosphate synthetase.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Although arginine is formed in the urea cycle, it is considered an essential amino-acid. Why?
questions.explanation: Although the urea cycle synthesizes arginine, the rate of endogenous synthesis is insufficient for the demands of rapid growth in infants and children, making it a conditionally essential amino acid during development. Adults normally synthesize adequate arginine.
questions.keyConcept: Arginine as conditionally essential amino acid in children
options: It must be broken down by arginase enzyme.
Its rate of synthesis is not enough for growing children.
It is formed in the cytosol, therefore it cannot be used.
It is formed in the D-configuration.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Two reactions of the urea cycle take place in the mitochondria. These are
questions.explanation: The first two reactions of the urea cycle occur in mitochondria: carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I forms carbamoyl phosphate, and ornithine transcarbamylase transfers the carbamoyl group to ornithine. The remaining reactions occur in the cytosol.
questions.keyConcept: Mitochondrial steps of urea cycle: CPS I and OTC
options: carbamoyl phosphate synthetase and ornithine transcarbamoylase.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is a high energy compound formed in the urea cycle?
questions.explanation: Carbamoyl phosphate is a high-energy compound formed in the first step of the urea cycle, consuming 2 ATP equivalents. It donates its energy to drive the subsequent reaction. Ornithine, citrulline, and argininosuccinate are not high-energy compounds.
questions.keyConcept: Carbamoyl phosphate as the high-energy intermediate of urea cycle

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following aminoacids is formed in the urea cycle and used in protein synthesis?
questions.explanation: Arginine is the only urea cycle intermediate that is incorporated into proteins; ornithine, citrulline, and argininosuccinate are not standard proteinogenic amino acids. Arginine is released when arginase cleaves argininosuccinate or directly from protein breakdown.
questions.keyConcept: Arginine as the only proteinogenic amino acid in urea cycle

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Ornithine is an aminoacid formed from
questions.explanation: Ornithine is produced from arginine by arginase and can be transaminated to glutamate via ornithine aminotransferase. Conversely, glutamate can be converted to ornithine through acetylation (N-acetylglutamate) and subsequent reactions in the urea cycle.
questions.keyConcept: Ornithine-glutamate interconversion in nitrogen metabolism
options: arginine and can be transformed to glutamate in two steps.
glutamate and can be transformed to arginine in the urea cycle.
arginine and transformed to aceto-acetate on fasting.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: N-acetyl-glutamate
questions.explanation: N-acetylglutamate (NAG) is synthesized from acetyl-CoA and glutamate by N-acetylglutamate synthase. NAG is an obligatory allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I), and its concentration increases after protein-rich meals when glutamate is abundant.
questions.keyConcept: NAG as allosteric activator of CPS I, increasing postprandially
options: is an allosteric activator of ornithine transcarbamoylase.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In the urea cycle, which aminoacids should be transported between the mitochondria and the cytosol in either direction?
questions.explanation: Ornithine must be transported from mitochondria to cytosol (where it combines with carbamoyl phosphate to form citrulline), and citrulline must travel back to mitochondria for the next step. This mitochondrial-cytosolic transport is essential for urea cycle function.
questions.keyConcept: Mitochondrial-cytosolic transport of ornithine and citrulline

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is produced by the urea cycle with the production of urea?
questions.explanation: The urea cycle produces fumarate when argininosuccinate is cleaved by argininosuccinase (argininosuccinate lyase). Fumarate can enter the TCA cycle or be converted to glucose via gluconeogenesis, linking the urea cycle to energy metabolism.
questions.keyConcept: Fumarate production from argininosuccinate in urea cycle

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The urea cycle is active in cases of
questions.explanation: Hepatocytes contain all five urea cycle enzymes: CPS I, OTC, ASS, ASL, and arginase. Extrahepatic tissues lack these enzymes and cannot synthesize urea, making the liver the sole organ for urea production. Deficiency causes hyperammonemia.
questions.keyConcept: Liver as exclusive site of urea cycle enzyme expression

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: How many carbon and nitrogen atoms are there in a urea molecule?
questions.explanation: Hyperammonemia inhibits alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase in the TCA cycle, diverting alpha-ketoglutarate to glutamate and then to glutamine synthesis. This disrupts brain energy metabolism and causes neurological symptoms, contributing to hepatic encephalopathy.
questions.keyConcept: Ammonia toxicity: inhibition of TCA cycle enzymes and glutamate accumulation

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is the source of urea carbon?
questions.explanation: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I) deficiency is the most common cause of hyperammonemia from urea cycle defects. Unlike CPS II (pyrimidine synthesis, not affected by NAG), CPS I requires N-acetylglutamate for activity, which is why NAG deficiency mimics CPS I deficiency.
questions.keyConcept: CPS I as rate-limiting enzyme requiring NAG for activation

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following gives one nitrogen atom of the urea molecule?
questions.explanation: Argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency (Citrullinemia type I) leads to citrulline accumulation. The diagnosis is confirmed by elevated citrulline in plasma and urine. This is the third enzyme of the urea cycle, encoding the ASS1 gene.
questions.keyConcept: Citrullinemia type I from ASS deficiency with citrulline elevation

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is a source of urea nitrogen?
questions.explanation: X-linked ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency is the most common urea cycle disorder. Males are more severely affected; female carriers may be asymptomatic or have mild symptoms. Plasma glutamine rises compensatorily when urea cycle is blocked.
questions.keyConcept: OTC deficiency as most common X-linked urea cycle disorder

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Glutamate can be the source of both nitrogen atoms of urea through which reactions?
questions.explanation: Glycine is broken down by the glycine cleavage system (P-protein, H-protein, T-protein, L-protein) in mitochondria. This system transfers the glycine amino group to pyridoxal phosphate, then releases CO2 and NH3, with the remaining carbon going to serine.
questions.keyConcept: Glycine cleavage system in mitochondria for glycine catabolism

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Ammonia is introduced in the urea cycle by
questions.explanation: Serine hydroxymethyltransferase (SHMT) catalyzes the reversible interconversion of serine and glycine in the cytosol and mitochondria. This reaction transfers a one-carbon unit to tetrahydrofolate, forming 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate, essential for nucleotide synthesis.
questions.keyConcept: Serine-glycine interconversion via SHMT generating one-carbon units
options: reacting as ammonium ion with carbon dioxide and ATP.
making a part of N-acetyl glutamate.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: How is carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I different from carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II?
questions.explanation: CPS I is mitochondrial and participates in the urea cycle (using ammonia and CO2), while CPS II is cytosolic and involved in pyrimidine synthesis (using glutamine). CPS I requires N-acetylglutamate as an allosteric activator; CPS II does not.
questions.keyConcept: CPS I (mitochondrial, urea cycle) vs CPS II (cytosolic, pyrimidine synthesis)
options: I is mitochondrial while II is cytosolic.
I is used for pyrimidine synthesis but II is for urea synthesis.
I does not need N-acetyl glutamate as allosteric activator, unlike II.
I uses glutamine not ammonia as a nitrogen donor.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is an energy-producing pathway?
questions.explanation: The citrate (Krebs) cycle produces energy by oxidizing acetyl-CoA, generating NADH, FADH2, and GTP. The urea cycle consumes energy (4 ATP equivalents) and does not produce ATP; its purpose is ammonia detoxification.
questions.keyConcept: Citric acid cycle as energy-producing pathway, urea cycle as energy-consuming

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: How many ATP (energy currency) are used in one turn of urea cycle?
questions.explanation: One turn of the urea cycle consumes 4 high-energy phosphate bonds: 2 ATP to form carbamoyl phosphate, 1 ATP to form argininosuccinate (AMP + PPi, counting as 2), with fumarate oxidation linking to the TCA cycle to recover some energy.
questions.keyConcept: Urea cycle energy cost: 4 ATP equivalents per turn

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following reactions linked to urea cycle may help covering its energy cost?
questions.explanation: The fumarate produced in the urea cycle enters the TCA cycle where malate dehydrogenase regenerates oxaloacetate, which is transaminated back to aspartate (used in argininosuccinate synthesis). Glutamate dehydrogenase and glutaminase provide ammonia for the cycle.
questions.keyConcept: TCA cycle link to urea cycle via fumarate and aspartate regeneration
options: Malate dehydrogenase involved in aspartate regeneration from fumarate.
Glutamate dehydrogenase involved in provision of ammonia.
Glutaminase involved in provision of ammonia.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: ATP is consumed in which of the following reactions?
questions.explanation: ATP is consumed in the CPS I reaction (2 ATP to 1 ADP) and the argininosuccinate synthetase reaction (ATP to AMP + PPi, effectively 2 ATP). Ornithine transcarbamylase does not require ATP; it transfers the carbamoyl group from carbamoyl phosphate to ornithine.
questions.keyConcept: ATP consumption at CPS I and ASS steps of urea cycle

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the use of glutamate for the urea cycle?
questions.explanation: Glutamate serves multiple roles: glutamate dehydrogenase provides ammonia (with NADPH), glutamate:oxaloacetate transaminase regenerates aspartate for argininosuccinate synthesis, and glutamate is the precursor for N-acetylglutamate synthesis.
questions.keyConcept: Glutamate as central nitrogen donor and NAG precursor for urea cycle
options: Production of ammonia by glutamate dehydrogenase reaction.
Regeneration of aspartate by the glutamate:oxaloacetate transaminase reaction.
Formation of the cycle activator: N-acetyl-glutamate.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: How is citric acid cycle useful for urea cycle?
questions.explanation: The TCA cycle generates ATP/GTP and also regenerates aspartate from fumarate through malate and oxaloacetate. Aspartate is required for argininosuccinate formation, linking these cycles. Thus both energy provision and anaplerosis connect them.
questions.keyConcept: TCA cycle support of urea cycle via energy and aspartate regeneration
options: Regeneration of aspartate from fumarate, through malate and oxalo-acetate.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is true about urea cycle?
questions.explanation: The urea cycle rate adapts to dietary protein content: higher protein intake increases amino acid deamination and ammonia production, upregulating urea cycle activity. It operates continuously, even during fasting when muscle protein breakdown releases nitrogen.
questions.keyConcept: Urea cycle rate variation with dietary protein intake
options: Its rate varies with the type of food.
Is not necessary in times of fasting.
The concentration of its enzymes is constant.
It is a closed pathway, with its intermediates not involved in other metabolic reactions.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which reaction of the urea cycle is the primary control reaction of the pathway?
questions.explanation: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I is the rate-limiting step of the urea cycle, controlled allosterically by N-acetylglutamate (NAG). This ensures the cycle activates only when ammonia and acetyl-CoA are available for detoxification.
questions.keyConcept: CPS I as rate-limiting, NAG-regulated step of urea cycle

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The rate of the urea cycle is controlled by
questions.explanation: Urea cycle rate is regulated at multiple levels: substrate (ammonia) availability stimulates CPS I, enzyme levels increase during high protein intake via induction, and arginine activates N-acetylglutamate synthase to boost CPS I activity.
questions.keyConcept: Multi-level regulation of urea cycle: substrate, induction, and allosteric control
options: arginine, which activates the synthesis of the allosteric activator.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Asparagine is important as
questions.explanation: Asparagine is critical for certain cancers (e.g., acute lymphoblastic leukemia) because they cannot synthesize it (lack asparagine synthetase) and require exogenous asparagine. Asparaginase enzyme therapy depletes circulating asparagine to starve tumor cells.
questions.keyConcept: Asparagine as essential requirement for certain cancer cells (asparaginase therapy)
options: an intermediate of the urea cycle.
an aminoacid that is formed by post-translational modification.
a primary source of ammonia in the kidney.
a requirement for certain cancer cells.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Match each description to the proper molecule:
questions.explanation: This is a matching question pairing molecule descriptions with their identities. The correct pairing is arginine producing urea on hydrolysis (arginine + H2O -> urea + ornithine via arginase). Understanding which urea cycle intermediate matches each description tests knowledge of the cycle's components.
questions.keyConcept: Urea cycle intermediates and their properties in matching format

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following is not true concerning codeine:
questions.explanation: Codeine is less likely than morphine to cause diarrhea as a troublesome side effect; both are constipating (opioid effect), but diarrhea is not a characteristic adverse effect of codeine. Codeine is actually used as an antidiarrheal in some formulations.
questions.keyConcept: Codeine side effects: antitussive, analgesic, constipating (not diarrheal)
options: Diarrhea is a troublesome side effect.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following is not common between pethidine & buprenorphine:
questions.explanation: Pethidine and buprenorphine differ in respiratory depression: pethidine causes dose-dependent respiratory depression, while buprenorphine (a partial agonist) has a ceiling effect on respiratory depression, making increased doses safer in this regard.
questions.keyConcept: Buprenorphine's ceiling effect on respiratory depression vs pethidine's dose-dependent effect
options: Respiratory depression is increased by increasing dose.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Pethidine differs from morphine in all the following Except:
questions.explanation: Pethidine is NOT preferred for long-term chronic pain management (unlike morphine). Both cause asphyxia neonatorum and biliary colic; pethidine has some atropine-like action. The exception is that pethidine is NOT used for long-term treatment.
questions.keyConcept: Pethidine NOT preferred for long-term chronic pain (unlike morphine) - EXCEPTION
options: It is preferred for long term treatment of chronic pain.
It is less liable to cause asphyxia neonatorum.
It is less liable to cause biliary colic.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following is NOT used in alcohol abuse
questions.explanation: Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine antagonist used for benzodiazepine overdose, not alcohol abuse. Disulfiram, acamprosate, and naltrexone are used for alcohol use disorder; thiamine prevents Wernicke encephalopathy in alcoholics.
questions.keyConcept: Flumazenil as benzodiazepine antagonist, not used in alcohol use disorder

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross Match each of the following to its adverse effect
questions.explanation: This matching question links adverse effects to CNS drugs: livid o reticularis with amantadine, fatal hepatotoxicity and hair thinning with valproate, and chest wall rigidity with fentanyl. These are characteristic adverse effect associations.
questions.keyConcept: Adverse effect matching: amantadine-livid o reticularis, valproate-hepatotoxicity, fentanyl-rigidity

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross Match each of the following drugs to its mechanism of action
questions.explanation: This matching covers antidepressant mechanisms: serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor = tramadol; dopamine-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor = bupropion; 5-HT1A partial agonist = buspirone; serotonin-norepinephrine releaser = mirtazapine.
questions.keyConcept: Antidepressant mechanism matching: SNRI, NDRI, 5-HT1A agonist, serotonin releaser

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following statements concerning anesthetics is correct ?
questions.explanation: Ketamine is a dissociative anesthetic that blocks NMDA (N-methyl-D-aspartate) glutamate receptors, producing anesthesia with catatonia and analgesia. Thiopental is short-acting due to redistribution, not metabolism; propofol lacks analgesic effect; halothane increases ICP.
questions.keyConcept: Ketamine as NMDA receptor antagonist producing dissociative anesthesia
options: Thiopental is ultra short acting due to rapid metabolism.
Propofol possesses a strong analgesic effect.
Halothane is the least likely inhalation agent to increase intracranial tension.
Dissociative anesthesia is induced by midazolam.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following concerning antiparkinsonian drugs is/are CORRECT?
questions.explanation: Apomorphine is given subcutaneously in Parkinson's disease emergencies (e.g., akinetic crisis), and amantadine can cause insomnia. Carbidopa does not reduce L-dopa-induced dyskinesia (dopamine agonists do). Benztropine is an anticholinergic for tremor, not fluctuations. Answer E (A and D) is correct.
questions.keyConcept: Apomorphine SC in emergency; amantadine-induced insomnia in Parkinson's treatment
options: Apomorphine is given subcutaneously in emergency.
L-dopa- induced dyskinesia is reduced by carbidopa.
Benztropine reduces fluctuations in response to L-dopa.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a NSAID? :
questions.explanation: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) is not an NSAID because it lacks significant anti-inflammatory activity; it has analgesic and antipyretic effects through different mechanisms (COX inhibition in brain, not peripheral). Aspirin, indomethacin, and ibuprofen are all NSAIDs with anti-inflammatory properties.
questions.keyConcept: Paracetamol as non-NSAID analgesic-antipyretic lacking anti-inflammatory activity

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which one of the following statements regarding NSAIDs is FALSE?
questions.explanation: Aspirin is contraindicated in children with viral infections due to Reye's syndrome risk; paracetamol or ibuprofen are preferred. All other statements about NSAIDs (nephrotoxicity, no respiratory depression, no dependence, GI irritation) are true.
questions.keyConcept: Aspirin contraindication in children (Reye's syndrome risk) making the statement FALSE
options: Nephrotoxicity may occur on chronic use of high doses
Respiratory depression seen with opioid analgesics does not occur with therapeutic doses of NSAIDs
Their use does not result in drug dependence seen with opioid analgesics
Aspirin is a good choice for use as analgesic antipyretic for children
They may cause-gastric mucosal irritation and bleeding

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following is common between aspirin and other NSAIDs
questions.explanation: Hypersensitivity reactions (bronchospasm, urticaria, anaphylaxis) can occur with any NSAID including aspirin due to shared COX inhibition and leukotriene pathway activation. Other listed effects are specific to aspirin (irreversible antiplatelet, MI prophylaxis) or vary among NSAIDs.
questions.keyConcept: Hypersensitivity as shared adverse effect of all NSAIDs including aspirin

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: NSAIDs are best avoided in:
questions.explanation: NSAIDs should be avoided in asthmatics (especially aspirin-induced asthma), patients with aspirin hypersensitivity, and those with GI bleeding history. All three represent absolute or relative contraindications to NSAID use.
questions.keyConcept: NSAID contraindications: asthma, aspirin allergy, and GI bleeding history
options: Patients with a history of gastric bleeding

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: All the following uses are shared by both aspirin and celecoxib EXCEPT
questions.explanation: Celecoxib (COX-2 inhibitor) lacks the antiplatelet effect of low-dose aspirin, so it is NOT used for MI prophylaxis. Both share anti-inflammatory use in musculoskeletal disorders, acute pain relief, and primary dysmenorrhea.
questions.keyConcept: Celecoxib lacks aspirin's cardiovascular antiplatelet prophylaxis indication
options: Anti-inflammatory in chronic inflammatory musculoskeletal disorders.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following analgesic agents poses a risk in a 60-year-old patient with a history of transient ischemic attacks
questions.explanation: Celecoxib (a COX-2 inhibitor) increases cardiovascular risk (thrombotic events, stroke) in patients with prior TIA or stroke history. Paracetamol and aspirin are safer options in such patients, with aspirin having protective antiplatelet effects.
questions.keyConcept: COX-2 inhibitors contraindicated in patients with prior TIA/stroke history

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is FALSE concerning selective COX 2 inhibitors ? :
questions.explanation: COX-2 inhibitors were withdrawn (rofecoxib) or carry warnings due to increased cardiovascular risk (heart attack, stroke). They do have low GI ulceration risk and nephrotoxicity concerns. Celecoxib is contraindicated in sulfonamide allergy.
questions.keyConcept: COX-2 inhibitors carry significant cardiovascular risk (heart attack, stroke) - FALSE statement
options: Are associated with low risk of gastric ulceration
Have a low risk of cardiotoxicity and stroke
Nephrotoxicity is a serious adverse effect
Celecoxib should not be given to patients with sulfonamide allergy

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following drug is NOT correctly matched to its side effects
questions.explanation: Ibuprofen is not associated with Reye's syndrome (that is aspirin's classic association in children with viral illness). Paracetamol does not cause bleeding (hepatotoxicity is the concern, not bleeding). Both B and D are incorrect matches, making E the answer.
questions.keyConcept: Ibuprofen is NOT associated with Reye's syndrome; paracetamol does not cause bleeding
options: Indomethacin/ severe headache due to cerebral VD.
Celecoxib/ rash since it is structurally related to sulfonamides.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following statements about aspirin is INCORRECT:
questions.explanation: Aspirin irreversibly inhibits COX enzymes (acetylation), not reversibly. This irreversible antiplatelet effect is why low-dose aspirin is used for cardiovascular prophylaxis. High doses cause tinnitus (salicylism), hyperuricemia, and GI bleeding.
questions.keyConcept: Aspirin's irreversible COX acetylation distinguishes it from reversible NSAID inhibition
options: It is mainly used today as a cardiovascular drug.
Inhibits platelet aggregation in low dose.
Tinnitus may occur with high dose

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which one of the following statements regarding paracetamol is TRUE? :
questions.explanation: The maximum recommended adult daily dose of paracetamol is 4 grams; exceeding this risks hepatotoxicity. Paracetamol is not excreted unchanged (hepatic metabolism), lacks anti-inflammatory action, and cross-reactivity with aspirin allergy is rare.
questions.keyConcept: Paracetamol maximum dose 4g/day; hepatotoxicity risk with overdose
options: It is excreted unchanged by the kidney
The maximum recommended daily dose in adults is 4 gm.
It should not be given in patient allergic to aspirin

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Concerning paracetamol, all are true Except:
questions.explanation: Paracetamol does not interfere with uric acid excretion (unlike aspirin which can either increase or decrease uric acid depending on dose). It is preferred in peptic ulcer, causes hepatic damage in overdose, and IV formulation exists for acute fever.
questions.keyConcept: Paracetamol does not affect uric acid excretion (not a uricosuric or anti-uricosuric)
options: Preferred to aspirin in peptic ulcer.
Acute paracetamol poisoning causes hepatic damage.
Interferes with excretion of uric acid.
May be used intravenously in acute fever of infectious origin.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following agent/s is/are used in transient ischemic attacks
questions.explanation: Low-dose aspirin (75-325mg daily) is the standard antiplatelet agent for secondary prevention in TIA. Warfarin is not routinely used for TIA; heparin is for acute events. Aspirin's antiplatelet effect prevents thromboembolic stroke recurrence.
questions.keyConcept: Low-dose aspirin as first-line antiplatelet for TIA secondary prevention

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross Match each of the following adverse effect to the corresponding drug
questions.explanation: This matching question links aplastic anemia and bleeding to indomethacin in osteoarthritis, though indomethacin is more associated with headache and GI effects. This question tests knowledge of NSAID adverse effect profiles in different clinical contexts.
questions.keyConcept: Indomethacin adverse effects: aplastic anemia, bleeding, headache, GI toxicity

pairs.target: D. Aspirin in transient ischemic attacks

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Chronic use of which of the following may increase paracetamol toxicity
questions.explanation: Rifampicin is a potent inducer of cytochrome P450 enzymes (especially CYP3A4) involved in paracetamol metabolism, increasing the production of toxic reactive metabolites (NAPQI). Chronic rifampicin use accelerates paracetamol hepatotoxicity by depleting glutathione faster.
questions.keyConcept: Rifampicin as CYP450 inducer increasing paracetamol hepatotoxicity risk

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following reversibly inhibits COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes?
questions.explanation: Ibuprofen reversibly inhibits both COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes, providing anti-inflammatory, analgesic, and antipyretic effects. Aspirin irreversibly acetylates COX; allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase (not COX); celecoxib selectively inhibits COX-2; sulphinpyrazone inhibits COX but is a uricosuric.
questions.keyConcept: Ibuprofen as reversible non-selective COX-1 and COX-2 inhibitor

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following is NOT true?
questions.explanation: Piroxicam has a long half-life (50 hours) allowing once-daily dosing, not three times daily. Diclofenac does exhibit efficacy between ibuprofen and indomethacin with a favorable side effect profile. Sulfinpyrazone can induce peptic ulcers and acute gout attacks by mobilizing uric acid.
questions.keyConcept: Piroxicam once-daily dosing due to long half-life (NOT three times daily)
options: Liver failure following paracetamol toxicity is due to glutathione depletion
Diclofenac exhibits higher efficacy than ibuprofen & less side effects than indomethacin
Probencid & sulfinpyrazone may induce acute attack of gout

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: This adverse effect is less with celecoxib compared to indomethacin
questions.explanation: Celecoxib (COX-2 selective) has a significantly lower risk of peptic ulcer disease compared to indomethacin (non-selective COX inhibitor) because COX-1 inhibition in the gastric mucosa reduces protective prostaglandin synthesis. All other listed effects (CV risk, nephrotoxicity, skin rash) are similar or worse with COX-2 inhibitors.
questions.keyConcept: COX-2 inhibitors have lower GI ulcer risk than non-selective NSAIDs like indomethacin

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Indomethacin is least likely to be prescribed in
questions.explanation: Indomethacin is a potent NSAID used for acute gout, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, and PDA closure. Osteoarthritis is typically managed with milder NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) or topical agents due to indomethacin's significant GI, CNS, and renal adverse effects.
questions.keyConcept: Indomethacin use in gout, RA, AS, PDA but avoided in osteoarthritis

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following poses the least risk of adverse cardiovascular events
questions.explanation: Naproxen has the lowest cardiovascular risk among traditional NSAIDs due to its relatively short half-life and less COX-2 selectivity. Piroxicam and diclofenac carry higher CV risk; indomethacin also increases blood pressure and CV events.
questions.keyConcept: Naproxen as NSAID with lowest cardiovascular adverse event risk

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Pain from ala of nose Is carried by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The external nasal nerve (branch of anterior ethmoidal nerve, which comes from the nasociliary nerve of V1) supplies the skin of the ala and tip of the nose. Infratrochlear supplies the medial angle; infraorbital supplies the lower eyelid and upper lip; buccal supplies the cheek.
questions.keyConcept: External nasal nerve supplies skin of ala and tip of nose

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Regarding the scalp the following statements are true Except:
questions.explanation: The large blood vessels of the scalp run in the subcutaneous connective tissue layer, which is the layer between the skin and epicranial aponeurosis. This layer contains fat and fibrous septae connecting skin to aponeurosis. Option B stating 'loose subaponeurotic space' is incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: Scalp blood vessels located in subcutaneous connective tissue, not subaponeurotic space
options: Infection from scalp wounds can spread to superior sagittal sinus.
Its blood vessels run in the loose subaponeurotic space.
Its skin, superficial fascia and aponeurosis move as one layer.
Frontal bellies of occipito-frontalis can corrugate skin of forehead.
Occipital bellies are supplied by facial nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The large blood vessels of scalp run into
questions.explanation: The large blood vessels of the scalp run in the subcutaneous connective tissue layer (between skin and aponeurosis). This layer has numerous anastomoses and lacks valves, allowing free blood flow. Injury causes profuse bleeding from this highly vascularized layer.
questions.keyConcept: Scalp vessels in subcutaneous connective tissue layer with extensive anastomoses

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following veins unite with a posterior a branch of the retromandibular vein to form external jugular vein?
questions.explanation: The posterior auricular vein joins the posterior branch of the retromandibular vein (formed by union of maxillary and superficial temporal veins) to form the external jugular vein. The facial vein drains into the common facial vein, then internal jugular.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior auricular vein unites with retromandibular vein to form external jugular

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The plane of movement of scalp is between:
questions.explanation: The plane of movement of the scalp is between the epicranial aponeurosis (galea aponeurotica) and the pericranium. This loose areolar tissue (dangerous area of scalp) allows the scalp to move over the skull. The other layers are more adherent to each other.
questions.keyConcept: Scalp movement plane between epicranial aponeurosis and pericranium (loose areolar tissue)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following nerves supplying scalp and face Is not derived from trigeminal nerve?
questions.explanation: The great auricular nerve (C2-C3) is derived from the cervical plexus, not the trigeminal nerve. It supplies the skin over the parotid gland and mastoid area. The auriculotemporal, zygomaticotemporal, supraorbital, and supratrochlear are all trigeminal branches.
questions.keyConcept: Great auricular nerve from C2-C3 cervical plexus, not trigeminal (V)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Loss of sensation from the lower eye lid indicates injury of which nerve?
questions.explanation: The infraorbital nerve (branch of maxillary division V2) provides sensory innervation to the skin of the lower eyelid, side of the nose, and upper lip via the infraorbital foramen. Injury causes loss of sensation in this distribution.
questions.keyConcept: Infraorbital nerve (V2) supplies lower eyelid sensation

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following muscles can produce transverse wrinkles in the forehead?
questions.explanation: The frontalis muscle (part of occipitofrontalis) pulls the scalp upward, producing transverse wrinkles across the forehead. Corrugator supercilii draws the eyebrow medially and downward (vertical frown lines); orbicularis oculi closes the eye.
questions.keyConcept: Frontalis muscle produces transverse forehead wrinkles by superior scalp pull

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Retromandibular vein:
questions.explanation: The retromandibular vein is formed by the union of the maxillary and superficial temporal veins, begins within the parotid gland, lies deep to the facial nerve within the parotid, and divides into anterior and posterior branches.
questions.keyConcept: Retromandibular vein formation, location in parotid gland, and division into branches
options: Is formed by union of maxillary & superficial temporal veins.
Is deep to facial nerve inside parotid gland.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Bleeding beneath the pericranium of the scalp:
questions.explanation: Bleeding beneath the pericranium (subperiosteal hematoma) is limited by the attachments of pericranium at suture lines, so it produces a swelling that conforms to the shape of the underlying bone (limited spread). This distinguishes it from the more diffuse swellings of other scalp layer hemorrhages.
questions.keyConcept: Subpericranial bleeding limited by suture lines, producing localized bony-shaped swelling
options: Spreads underneath all of the scalp.
Makes a swelling that takes the shape of the underlying bone.
Reaches to the back of neck.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The motor nerve of the scalp behind the auricle is:
questions.explanation: The posterior auricular branch of the facial nerve supplies the occipital belly of occipitofrontalis and the small muscles around the external ear behind the auricle. The temporal branch supplies the frontalis and orbicularis oculi.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior auricular branch of facial nerve supplies scalp muscles behind auricle
options: Posterior auricular branch of facial nerve.
Marginal mandibular branch of facial nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Lymph from central part of upper lip drop, directly to:
questions.explanation: Lymph from the central part of the upper lip (philtrum area) drains directly to the submental lymph nodes, located beneath the chin between the anterior bellies of the digastric muscles. This is part of the facial lymph drainage system.
questions.keyConcept: Central upper lip drains directly to submental lymph nodes

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Buccinator:
questions.explanation: The buccinator muscle arises from both the outer surfaces of the maxilla and mandible (alveolar processes), as well as the pterygomandibular raphe. It is a muscle of facial expression (not mastication), compressed by the buccinator to keep food between teeth.
questions.keyConcept: Buccinator arises from both maxilla and mandible; it is a muscle of facial expression
options: Is one of the muscles of mastication.
Is supplied by buccal branch of mandibular nerve.
Arises from both mandible and maxilla.
Is covered by investing layer of fascia.
Accumulates food in vestibule of mouth.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The branch of the mandibular nerve that supplies the scalp is the:
questions.explanation: The auriculotemporal nerve (branch of V3) provides sensory innervation to the scalp region above and in front of the ear (temporal region). It carries postganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the otic ganglion to the parotid gland.
questions.keyConcept: Auriculotemporal nerve (V3) supplies the scalp above and anterior to the ear

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Internal carotid artery supplies:
questions.explanation: The forehead is supplied by the supratrochlear and supraorbital arteries, which are branches of the internal carotid artery (via the ophthalmic artery). The chin and cheek are supplied by facial artery; the non-hairy temple by superficial temporal artery.
questions.keyConcept: Forehead supplied by internal carotid branches (supraorbital, supratrochlear arteries)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The scalp Is:
questions.explanation: The scalp behind the auricle is supplied by the lesser occipital nerve, derived from the ventral ramus of C2 (not C3). The greater occipital nerve (C2 dorsal ramus) supplies the back of the scalp. The supratrochlear and supraorbital are from the internal carotid system.
questions.keyConcept: Lesser occipital nerve (ventral ramus C2) supplies scalp behind auricle
options: Supplied by the great auricular nerve in front of the auricle.
Supplied by the supratrochlear and supraorbital arteries branches of the facial artery.
Supplied posteriorly by the greater occipital nerve from the ventral ramus of C2.
Supplied behind the auricle by the lesser occipital nerve from the ventral ramus of C2.
Drained by supratrochlear and supraorbital veins, which unite to form the superior ophthalmic vein.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The upper lip:
questions.explanation: All statements about the upper lip are correct: it is supplied by the facial artery (via superior labial branch), maxillary nerve (via infraorbital), lies in the dangerous area of face (connects to cavernous sinus), and the philtrum can be obliterated by infection tracking along the angular vein.
questions.keyConcept: Upper lip supplied by facial artery and V2, lies in dangerous area of face
options: Lies in the dangerous area of face.
Its philtrum is obliterated in infections.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Facial artery:
questions.explanation: The facial artery has a tortuous course to accommodate neck and facial movements without tension. It is a branch of the external carotid artery (not internal), enters the face at the antero-inferior angle of the buccinator, and ends at the side of the nose as the angular artery.
questions.keyConcept: Facial artery is tortuous, external carotid branch, enters face at buccinator angle
options: Is a branch of internal carotid artery
Enters face at antero-inferior angle of Buccinator
Ends by anastomosing with supraorbital artery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following contains parasympathetic postganglionic fibers?
questions.explanation: The auriculotemporal nerve carries parasympathetic postganglionic fibers from the otic ganglion (via the lesser petrosal nerve pathway) to the parotid gland. These secretomotor fibers stimulate salivary secretion. The tympanic nerve and lesser petrosal carry preganglionic fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Auriculotemporal nerve carries parasympathetic fibers to parotid gland from otic ganglion

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The nerve supply of the muscle of the scalp is:
questions.explanation: The muscles of the scalp (occipitofrontalis, orbicularis oculi, corrugator supercilii) are muscles of facial expression and are innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII). The trigeminal nerve provides sensory innervation, not motor to these muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Scalp muscles innervated by facial nerve (CN VII), not trigeminal

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Pulse felt at antero-inferior angle of masseter is from which artery?
questions.explanation: The pulse felt at the antero-inferior angle of the masseter muscle (over the mandible) is from the facial artery, which crosses over the mandible at this point. The facial artery is commonly used for checking pulse and taking blood pressure in some settings.
questions.keyConcept: Facial artery pulse palpable at antero-inferior angle of masseter (over mandible)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Infection from dangerous area of face may be transmitted to the following venous sinus:
questions.explanation: The 'dangerous area of face' refers to the region around the nose, upper lip, and orbit where infections can spread via the facial vein (which has no valves) to the cavernous sinus. This causes cavernous sinus thrombosis.
questions.keyConcept: Dangerous area of face connects to cavernous sinus via valveless facial vein

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: In which of the following layers of the scalp does infection tend to spread:
questions.explanation: Infection spreads easily in the loose areolar tissue layer (between aponeurosis and pericranium) because it has little structural resistance. This is why it is called the 'dangerous layer' of the scalp - infections here can spread to intracranial structures.
questions.keyConcept: Loose areolar tissue layer is the dangerous layer where scalp infections spread

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Pain from upper lip is carried by.
questions.explanation: The infraorbital nerve (V2 branch) provides sensory innervation to the skin of the upper lip. The buccal nerve supplies the buccal mucosa (not skin) of the cheek; mental nerve supplies the lower lip; zygomaticofacial supplies the malar region.
questions.keyConcept: Infraorbital nerve (V2) carries sensation from upper lip skin

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Infection of lateral part of the upper eye lid leads to enlargement of this group of lymph nodes:
questions.explanation: The lateral part of the upper eyelid drains to the preauricular (parotid) lymph nodes. The medial part drains to the submandibular nodes. This is clinically relevant for spread of eyelid infections and tumors.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral upper eyelid drains to parotid (preauricular) lymph nodes

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Bleeding in which layer of scalp causes black eye?
questions.explanation: Bleeding in the loose areolar tissue layer (between aponeurosis and pericranium) can track along the emissary veins to the eyelid, producing the characteristic 'black eye' or periorbital ecchymosis. This layer connects to the upper eyelid.
questions.keyConcept: Loose areolar tissue bleeding tracks to eyelids causing black eye (raccoon eyes)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The lowermost soft part of the auricle of ear is called:
questions.explanation: The lobule is the soft, non-cartilaginous inferior part of the auricle consisting of fibrofatty tissue. The tragus is the cartilaginous projection anterior to the external auditory meatus; the concha is the deep cartilaginous cavity.
questions.keyConcept: Lobule of ear is the soft, non-cartilaginous lower part (fibrofatty tissue)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The nerve that carries the sensation for the lower eyelid is:
questions.explanation: The infraorbital nerve (terminal branch of V2, maxillary division) provides sensory innervation to the lower eyelid. It exits via the infraorbital foramen and supplies the skin and conjunctiva of the lower eyelid.
questions.keyConcept: Infraorbital nerve (V2) supplies lower eyelid sensation

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Regarding Scalp, all are true Except:
questions.explanation: The scalp does contain sebaceous glands (especially associated with hair follicles), making option C false. The scalp has profuse bleeding due to anastomosing arteries, gapes when aponeurosis is cut due to muscle pull, connects to intracranial sinuses via emissary veins, and contains frontalis muscle (facial expression).
questions.keyConcept: Scalp contains sebaceous glands (false statement about scalp anatomy)
options: Its wounds gape if the aponeurosis is cut.
Its veins communicate with the intracranial Venous sinuses.
It contains a muscle of facial expression.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The non-hairy region of the temple is supplied by which of the following nerves?
questions.explanation: The zygomaticotemporal nerve (branch of zygomatic nerve from V2) supplies the skin over the non-hairy temple (anterior temporal region). The auriculotemporal supplies the hairy temple region. The infratrochlear and infraorbital supply the nose and upper lip area.
questions.keyConcept: Zygomaticotemporal nerve (V2) supplies non-hairy temple region

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The main sensory nerve to the lower lip Is the:
questions.explanation: The mental nerve (terminal branch of the inferior alveolar nerve, a V3 branch) provides sensory innervation to the skin of the lower lip and chin. It exits through the mental foramen on the mandible.
questions.keyConcept: Mental nerve (V3 branch) provides main sensory supply to lower lip

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Infection of scalp area behind the ear affects which group of LNs
questions.explanation: The scalp area behind the ear (posterior to the auricle) drains to the occipital lymph nodes, located near the attachment of trapezius at the base of the skull. These nodes also receive drainage from the back of the scalp.
questions.keyConcept: Occipital lymph nodes drain scalp behind the ear

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is sensory to the scalp behind the auricle?
questions.explanation: The great auricular nerve (C2-C3, from cervical plexus) provides sensory innervation to the skin behind the auricle and the parotid region. The auriculotemporal nerve supplies the temple; superficial temporal nerve supplies the scalp above the ear.
questions.keyConcept: Great auricular nerve (C2-C3) provides sensation behind the auricle

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All of the following regarding orbicularis oris muscle is correct Except:
questions.explanation: The orbicularis oris is a composite muscle formed by fibers from multiple facial muscles (caninus, trapezius, incisivus superior/inferior) that converge at the modiolus, not a complete circular sphincter. The orbicularis oculi is the true sphincter around the eye.
questions.keyConcept: Orbicularis oris is NOT a complete circular sphincter; it is composite at modiolus
options: It is a muscle of facial expression.
It is supplied by facial nerve.
Its fibers form complete circles around the mouth.
It can close the oral (labial) fissure.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The nerve supplying the buccinator muscle is:
questions.explanation: The buccinator muscle is a muscle of facial expression and is innervated by the buccal branches of the facial nerve (CN VII). The buccal nerve of V3 provides sensory innervation to the cheek mucosa, not motor function to the muscle.
questions.keyConcept: Buccinator motor supply by facial nerve (CN VII), not mandibular nerve

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The following is a branch of the superficial temporal artery in the face:
questions.explanation: The transverse facial artery is a branch of the superficial temporal artery that runs horizontally across the face beneath the zygomatic arch. The supraorbital, supratrochlear, infraorbital, and inferior labial arteries are from the ophthalmic or facial arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Transverse facial artery is branch of superficial temporal artery in the face

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The 2 frontal bellies:
questions.explanation: The two frontal bellies of occipitofrontalis are separated from each other by the galea aponeurotica and are joined at the median plane. They originate from the skin of the eyebrow region, are supplied by the supraorbital nerve, and attach to the superior temporal line.
questions.keyConcept: Frontal bellies are separated from each other in the midline
options: Form the only muscle of face.
Are attached to superior temporal line.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Regarding buccinator muscle, all the following statements are true Except:
questions.explanation: The buccinator is covered by the mucosa of the cheek (not buccopharyngeal fascia), which is the correct answer making it the false statement. The buccopharyngeal fascia covers the constrictor muscles of the pharynx. The buccinator arises from maxilla, mandible, and pterygomandibular raphe.
questions.keyConcept: Buccinator covered by mucosa, not buccopharyngeal fascia (false statement)
options: It arises from both maxilla and mandible.
The pterygomandibular raphe is a common origin for this muscle and the middle constrictor.
Its middle fibers decussate at the modiolus.
It is covered by buccopharyngeal fascia.
It compresses the cheeks against the teeth.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Lacrimal part of orbicularis oculi:
questions.explanation: The lacrimal part of orbicularis oculi (Homer-Wright muscle) is attached to the medial palpebral ligament and the lacrimal fascia. It helps spread tears and is involved in the lacrimal pump mechanism. It is supplied by the facial nerve, not auriculotemporal.
questions.keyConcept: Lacrimal part of orbicularis oculi attached to medial palpebral ligament, involved in lacrimal pump
options: Is attached to medial palpebral ligament.
Is attached to lateral palpebral raphe.
Is a part of orbicularis oris.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Regarding lips all are true Except:
questions.explanation: The main sensory supply to the upper lip is the infraorbital nerve (V2 branch), NOT the facial nerve which is motor. The mental nerve supplies the lower lip. The facial nerve provides motor innervation to lip muscles, not sensory.
questions.keyConcept: Upper lip sensory supply is V2 (infraorbital), not facial nerve - FALSE statement
options: The main sensory supply to upper lip is facial nerve.
The main sensory supply to lower lip is Mental nerve.
Their muscles are formed mainly by orbicularis oris.
Their blood supply is through facial artery.
In facial palsy lips can’t be dilated.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The branch of facial nerve that supplies the platysma is the
questions.explanation: The platysma (a facial expression muscle in the neck) is supplied by the cervical branch of the facial nerve. This branch also innervates the orbicularis oris and the lower lip muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Cervical branch of facial nerve supplies platysma

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Mandibular nerve is sensory to:
questions.explanation: The mandibular nerve (V3) provides sensory innervation to the lower lip via the mental nerve (terminal branch of inferior alveolar nerve). The upper eyelid and lower eyelid are V1/V2 territories; the tip of nose is V1; upper lip is V2.
questions.keyConcept: Mandibular nerve (V3) sensory to lower lip via mental nerve

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Pulse felt in front of tragus of ear against zygomatic arch is from which artery?
questions.explanation: The pulse palpable in front of the tragus against the zygomatic arch is from the superficial temporal artery (terminal branch of external carotid). This is a common site for checking pulse and temporal artery biopsy.
questions.keyConcept: Superficial temporal artery pulse palpable anterior to tragus

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The anterior triangle of the neck, include the following Except one:
questions.explanation: The occipital triangle is part of the posterior triangle of the neck, not the anterior triangle. The anterior triangle subdivisions include muscular, carotid, digastric, and submental triangles.
questions.keyConcept: Occipital triangle is in posterior triangle, not anterior triangle - EXCEPTION

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Regarding digastric triangle. All are true Except:
questions.explanation: The digastric triangle is bounded by the inferior border of the mandible superiorly (not the hyoid bone), the anterior belly of digastric anteriorly, and the posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid posteriorly.
questions.keyConcept: Digastric triangle bounded superiorly by mandible, not hyoid bone - FALSE statement
options: It is bounded anteriorly by anterior belly of digastric.
It is bounded posteriorly by posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid.
It is bounded superiorly by hyoid bone.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following muscles subdivides the posterior triangle of the neck:
questions.explanation: The inferior belly of the omohyoid muscle subdivides the posterior triangle into an occipital triangle (above) and a supraclavicular triangle (below). The sternocleidomastoid forms the anterior border; the superior belly of omohyoid is within the anterior triangle.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior belly of omohyoid subdivides posterior triangle into two parts

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The following muscle bounds the carotid triangle posteriorly:
questions.explanation: The sternocleidomastoid muscle forms the posterior boundary of the carotid triangle. The anterior border is the superior belly of omohyoid; the posterior border is the sternocleidomastoid; the floor is formed by the longus colli, scalene muscles, and levator scapulae.
questions.keyConcept: Sternocleidomastoid forms posterior boundary of carotid triangle

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The following structures form the floor of the posterior triangle of the neck Except:
questions.explanation: The floor of the posterior triangle is formed by the levator scapulae, splenius capitis, and scalenus medius muscles, covered by the prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia. The investing layer surrounds the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid, not forming the floor.
questions.keyConcept: Investing layer of deep cervical fascia is NOT part of floor of posterior triangle - EXCEPTION
options: Investing layer of deep cervical fascia.
Prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The cutaneous nerve supply over the anterior triangle of the neck is largely from:
questions.explanation: The transverse cutaneous nerve of the neck (from C2-C3, cervical plexus) provides the main cutaneous sensory supply to the anterior triangle of the neck. The great auricular nerve supplies the lateral neck; dorsal rami supply the posterior neck.
questions.keyConcept: Transverse cutaneous nerve of neck (C2-C3) supplies anterior triangle skin sensation

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Six hours after a meal, which of the following is (are) MOST important as a source of fuel for the brain?
questions.explanation: Six hours after a meal, the brain relies primarily on ketone bodies (acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate) produced by the liver from fatty acid oxidation. Glycogen stores are depleted by then; fatty acids cannot cross the blood-brain barrier; muscle protein is a gluconeogenic substrate, not direct fuel.
questions.keyConcept: Six hours post-meal, ketone bodies become the major brain fuel
options: Fatty acids from the adipose tissue.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is an absolute requirement for the brain at all times?
questions.explanation: The brain absolutely requires both glucose and oxygen at all times. Unlike other organs, the brain cannot use fatty acids (blood-brain barrier restriction) and depends entirely on glucose via GLUT transporters. Ketone bodies can substitute partially during prolonged starvation.
questions.keyConcept: Glucose and oxygen are absolute requirements for brain function at all times

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In fasting conditions, glucose is provided for the brain by:
questions.explanation: In fasting, liver glycogen is depleted within 12-18 hours, after which hepatic gluconeogenesis (from lactate, glycerol, and amino acids) becomes the primary source of glucose for the brain. Intestinal absorption is minimal 6 hours post-meal.
questions.keyConcept: Hepatic gluconeogenesis becomes primary glucose source for brain during fasting

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Brain cells uptake glucose by:
questions.explanation: Brain cells take up glucose via GLUT1 (on the blood-brain barrier, constitutive) and GLUT3 (on neurons, high affinity). GLUT2 is in liver and pancreas; GLUT4 is insulin-dependent (muscle/fat); GLUT5 is a fructose transporter; SGLT2 is in kidney.
questions.keyConcept: Brain glucose uptake by GLUT1 (BBB) and GLUT3 (neurons)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In carcinoid syndrome the argentaffin tissue of the abdominal cavity overproduce:
questions.explanation: In carcinoid syndrome, the argentaffin (enterochromaffin) cells of the gut overproduce serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine) from tryptophan. This causes the characteristic symptoms: diarrhea, flushing, and cardiac valvular fibrosis.
questions.keyConcept: Carcinoid syndrome overproduces serotonin from argentaffin cells

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The rate limiting step in the biosynthesis of catecholamines is:
questions.explanation: Tyrosine hydroxylase catalyzes the hydroxylation of tyrosine to DOPA, which is the rate-limiting step in catecholamine biosynthesis. This enzyme requires tetrahydrobiopterin as cofactor and is feedback-inhibited by catecholamines.
questions.keyConcept: Tyrosine hydroxylase as rate-limiting enzyme in catecholamine biosynthesis

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following amine acids may act as a neurotransmitter?
questions.explanation: Glycine, glutamic acid (glutamate), and GABA are the three major amino acid neurotransmitters in the CNS. Glycine is inhibitory in spinal cord; glutamate is the main excitatory neurotransmitter; GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter.
questions.keyConcept: Glycine, glutamate, and GABA as the three major amino acid neurotransmitters

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The enzyme dopamine beta-oxidase (hydroxylase) which catalyzes conversion of dopamine to norepinephrine requires:
questions.explanation: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase requires vitamin C (ascorbic acid) as a cofactor for the hydroxylation of dopamine to norepinephrine. The enzyme also contains copper. This is why ascorbate deficiency can impair catecholamine synthesis.
questions.keyConcept: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase requires vitamin C (ascorbic acid) as cofactor

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Histamine is formed from histidine by:
questions.explanation: Histidine is decarboxylated by histidine decarboxylase to form histamine. This is analogous to other neurotransmitter synthesis (DOPA to dopamine, 5-HTP to serotonin). Histamine is stored in mast cells and brain neurons.
questions.keyConcept: Histidine decarboxylation produces histamine

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A vasodilating compound is produced by the decarboxylation of the amino acid:
questions.explanation: Histidine decarboxylation produces histamine, which is a potent vasodilator. Histamine acts on H1 receptors causing vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, and bronchoconstriction.
questions.keyConcept: Histidine decarboxylation produces vasodilator histamine

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Gamma-amino-butyric acid (GABA) is produced by:
questions.explanation: GABA is produced by decarboxylation of glutamic acid (glutamate) via glutamate decarboxylase (GAD), which requires pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) as a cofactor. This is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS.
questions.keyConcept: GABA synthesis from glutamate via GAD requiring PLP (B6) cofactor
options: A reaction that requires vitamin B6 derived cofactor.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The defective enzyme in histidinemia is:
questions.explanation: Histidinemia is caused by a deficiency of histidase (histidine ammonia-lyase), which normally converts histidine to urocanic acid. This is a rare autosomal recessive disorder presenting with intellectual disability and speech defects.
questions.keyConcept: Histidase deficiency causes histidinemia (histidine ammonia-lyase)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Serotonin is synthesized from:
questions.explanation: Serotonin is synthesized from the essential amino acid tryptophan via hydroxylation (tryptophan hydroxylase) to 5-hydroxytryptophan, then decarboxylation (ALAD) to serotonin (5-HT). Tryptophan hydroxylase requires tetrahydrobiopterin.
questions.keyConcept: Serotonin synthesized from tryptophan (not tyrosine or phenylalanine)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following increases in 24 Hour urine with pheochromocytoma (adrenaline-secreting tumor)?
questions.explanation: Pheochromocytoma secretes excess catecholamines (epinephrine/norepinephrine), which are metabolized to vanillylmandelic acid (VMA). VMA is measured in 24-hour urine as the primary diagnostic marker for this tumor.
questions.keyConcept: VMA elevated in 24-hour urine with pheochromocytoma

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following may be measured in 24-hour urine to diagnose carcinoid syndrome (argentaffinoma, serotonin secreting tumor)?
questions.explanation: Carcinoid syndrome (argentaffinoma) overproduces serotonin, which is metabolized to 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA). Elevated 24-hour urinary 5-HIAA is the standard diagnostic test for carcinoid syndrome.
questions.keyConcept: 5-HIAA in 24-hour urine is diagnostic for carcinoid syndrome

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following may serve as a tumor marker?
questions.explanation: Both VMA (from pheochromocytoma, measuring catecholamine catabolism) and 5-HIAA (from carcinoid tumors, measuring serotonin catabolism) serve as tumor markers when measured in 24-hour urine collections.
questions.keyConcept: VMA and 5-HIAA both serve as neuroendocrine tumor markers

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following enzymes is important for synthesis of both epinephrine and melatonin?
questions.explanation: Aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (ALAD) is required for synthesis of both catecholamines (DOPA to dopamine) and melatonin (5-HTP to serotonin). Dihydrobiopterin reductase is also involved in catecholamine synthesis.
questions.keyConcept: ALAD is common enzyme in both catecholamine and melatonin synthesis pathways

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Methyl dopa decreases blood pressure by:
questions.explanation: Alpha-methyl-dopa (methyldopa) decreases blood pressure by acting as a false neurotransmitter: it is converted to methyl-norepinephrine which displaces norepinephrine from sympathetic nerve terminals, reducing sympathetic outflow.
questions.keyConcept: Methyldopa acts as false neurotransmitter displacing norepinephrine to reduce BP

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is true about the amino acid neurotransmitters?
questions.explanation: All statements about amino acid neurotransmitters are correct: glutamate is excitatory, glycine and GABA are inhibitory; glycine constitutes one-third of collagen; glutamic acid is produced from other amino acids; monosodium glutamate is a widely used food additive.
questions.keyConcept: All statements about amino acid neurotransmitters are true: glutamate excitatory, glycine/GABA inhibitory
options: Glutamic acid is an excitatory, while Glycine and GABA are inhibitory neurotransmitters.
Glycine constitutes one third of the collagen amino acids, and glutamic acid is largely produced from other amino acids.
Monosodium glutamate is a widely used food additive.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Histamine is formed from histidine by which of the following enzymes or reactions:
questions.explanation: Histamine is formed from histidine by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (ALAD), which requires pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) as a cofactor. This reaction is analogous to other decarboxylations in neurotransmitter synthesis.
questions.keyConcept: Histidine decarboxylase (ALAD) requires PLP to form histamine from histidine
options: A reaction that requires pyridoxal phosphate.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Nitric Oxide is a hormone and a neurotransmitter synthesized:
questions.explanation: Nitric oxide (NO) is synthesized by nitric oxide synthase from the amino acid arginine (not glycine), producing citrulline and NO. NO acts as a gaseous neurotransmitter and vasodilator.
questions.keyConcept: Nitric oxide synthase converts arginine (not glycine) to NO and citrulline
options: By the action of nitric oxide synthase.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: GABA (gamma amino butyric acid) is:
questions.explanation: GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS, acting on GABA-A (ionotropic, chloride channel) and GABA-B (metabotropic, G-protein coupled) receptors. It is produced postsynaptically from glutamate by GAD.
questions.keyConcept: GABA is the major postsynaptic inhibitory neurotransmitter in CNS

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Mono Amine Oxidase (MAO) catalyzes the conversion of serotonin to:
questions.explanation: MAO converts serotonin to 5-hydroxyindoleacetaldehyde, which is then oxidized by aldehyde dehydrogenase to 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA). This is the primary metabolite measured for carcinoid tumor diagnosis.
questions.keyConcept: MAO converts serotonin to 5-HIAA via aldehyde intermediate

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: L-Dopa (Dihydroxyphenylalanine) is:
questions.explanation: L-dopa (dihydroxyphenylalanine) is produced by hydroxylation of tyrosine (not decarboxylation of noradrenaline), catalyzed by tyrosine hydroxylase. It is then converted to dopamine by DOPA decarboxylase (aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase).
questions.keyConcept: L-dopa formed by tyrosine hydroxylation, not noradrenaline decarboxylation
options: Converted to tyrosine by a hydroxylase enzyme.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The rate-limiting step in catecholamine synthesis is:
questions.explanation: The hydroxylation of tyrosine to DOPA by tyrosine hydroxylase is the rate-limiting step in catecholamine synthesis. This enzyme requires tetrahydrobiopterin as cofactor and is feedback-inhibited by the end products.
questions.keyConcept: Tyrosine hydroxylase catalyzes rate-limiting step in catecholamine synthesis

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Decarboxylation of 5-hydroxytryptophan results in formation of:
questions.explanation: Decarboxylation of 5-hydroxytryptophan by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (ALAD) produces serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine, 5-HT). This is the second step in serotonin biosynthesis, after tryptophan hydroxylation.
questions.keyConcept: 5-hydroxytryptophan decarboxylation produces serotonin (5-HT)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Serotonin is:
questions.explanation: Serotonin is 5-hydroxytryptamine, synthesized from tryptophan (not a tyrosine derivative). Melatonin is produced from serotonin by N-acetylation and O-methylation, not the reverse pathway.
questions.keyConcept: Serotonin is 5-HT, an indoleamine from tryptophan, not tyrosine
options: Produced by N-acetylation and methylation of melatonin.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Serotonin is catabolized by:
questions.explanation: Serotonin is primarily catabolized by monoamine oxidase (MAO), which oxidatively deaminates it to 5-hydroxyindoleacetaldehyde. This is further oxidized to 5-HIAA. COMT does not significantly metabolize serotonin.
questions.keyConcept: MAO is the primary catabolic enzyme for serotonin

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Vitamin B-derived coenzyme is needed for the synthesis of which of the following?
