questions.explanation: Dopamine is converted from L-dopa by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (ALAD), which requires pyridoxal phosphate (PLP, B6) as a cofactor. PNMT (for epinephrine from norepinephrine) uses SAM; melatonin from serotonin does not require B6-derived cofactor.
questions.keyConcept: ALAD requires PLP (B6) to convert L-dopa to dopamine

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Melatonin is synthesized from which of the following?
questions.explanation: Melatonin is synthesized from tryptophan via the pathway: tryptophan -> 5-hydroxytryptophan -> serotonin -> N-acetylserotonin -> melatonin. It is produced by the pineal gland and regulates circadian rhythms.
questions.keyConcept: Melatonin synthesized from tryptophan (not tyrosine, melanin, or MSH)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is a tumor marker that indicates high adrenaline secretion?
questions.explanation: Urinary vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) is the end product of catecholamine catabolism and is elevated in patients with pheochromocytoma (adrenaline-secreting tumor). This is the standard biochemical screening test.
questions.keyConcept: VMA in urine as tumor marker for pheochromocytoma (adrenaline-secreting tumor)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Catecholamines are:
questions.explanation: Catecholamines (dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine) function both as circulating hormones (from adrenal medulla) and as neurotransmitters (in the CNS and sympathetic nervous system). They contain the catechol ring structure.
questions.keyConcept: Catecholamines function as both circulating hormones and neurotransmitters

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Regarding the structure of catecholamines:
questions.explanation: Catecholamines contain the catechol (3,4-dihydroxyphenyl) ring structure and are synthesized from the amino acid tyrosine, not glycine. The catechol ring is essential for their biological activity.
questions.keyConcept: Catecholamines contain catechol ring, synthesized from tyrosine
options: Contain the catechol (3,4-dihydroxyphenyl) ring in their structure.
Are synthesized from the amino acid glycine.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following reactions produces carbon dioxide?
questions.explanation: Serotonin synthesis from 5-hydroxytryptophan by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase produces CO2 as a byproduct of the decarboxylation reaction. Acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA (fatty acid synthesis) also produces CO2.
questions.keyConcept: Decarboxylation of 5-HTP to serotonin produces carbon dioxide
options: Conversion of acetyl CoA to malonyl CoA.
Synthesis of serotonin from its precursor.
Action of monoamine oxidase on norepinephrine.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is measured in the urine to confirm the presence of an adrenaline secreting tumor?
questions.explanation: Vanillomandelic acid (VMA) in urine confirms pheochromocytoma, as it is the major end product of adrenaline and noradrenaline metabolism. Elevated urinary VMA is a sensitive screening test for this tumor.
questions.keyConcept: Vanillomandelic acid (VMA) in urine confirms adrenaline-secreting tumor

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Norepinephrine is produced by:
questions.explanation: Norepinephrine is produced by hydroxylation of dopamine via dopamine beta-hydroxylase. This enzyme requires vitamin C (ascorbic acid), copper, and tetrahydrobiopterin as cofactors.
questions.keyConcept: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase hydroxylates dopamine to form norepinephrine

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Production of norepinephrine from dopamine requires:
questions.explanation: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase is a copper-containing oxidase that hydroxylates dopamine to norepinephrine. It requires vitamin C as an electron donor and tetrahydrobiopterin as a cofactor. Both a and b are correct.
questions.keyConcept: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase requires copper, vitamin C, and tetrahydrobiopterin

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Hormones and neurotransmitters:
questions.explanation: Hormones and neurotransmitters are signal molecules for cell-cell communication, mostly derived from amino acids (polypeptides, nitrogenous compounds). Non-nitrogenous signal molecules (like steroid hormones, fatty acid derivatives) also exist.
questions.keyConcept: Signal molecules include both nitrogenous and non-nitrogenous compounds
options: Are signal molecules used for cell-cell communication.
Are mostly polypeptides or nitrogenous compounds, both derived from amino acids.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Vitamin B6 is important for which of the following regarding brain metabolism?
questions.explanation: Vitamin B6 (pyridoxal phosphate) is essential for synthesizing major neurotransmitters: dopamine, norepinephrine, serotonin, GABA, and histamine, all produced by PLP-dependent decarboxylation reactions.
questions.keyConcept: Vitamin B6 (PLP) required for synthesis of major CNS neurotransmitters
options: Detoxification of ammonia by formation of glutamine.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The end product of adrenaline and noradrenaline catabolism is:
questions.explanation: Vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) is the primary urinary metabolite of both epinephrine and norepinephrine. It is formed through combined MAO and COMT action and is routinely measured as a diagnostic marker for pheochromocytoma.
questions.keyConcept: VMA as end product of adrenaline and noradrenaline catabolism

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: To increase the synthesis of catecholamines in the brain, a patient with Parkinsonism may be given:
questions.explanation: L-dopa crosses the blood-brain barrier and is converted to dopamine by DOPA decarboxylase, increasing catecholamine levels in Parkinson's patients with dopaminergic neuron loss. Alpha-methyldopa is an antihypertensive.
questions.keyConcept: L-dopa administered to increase brain catecholamine synthesis in Parkinson's disease

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following coenzymes is required for the synthesis of GABA, serotonin, and histamine from their respective amino acid precursors?
questions.explanation: Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP, vitamin B6) is the cofactor for decarboxylation reactions that produce GABA (from glutamate), serotonin (from 5-HTP), and histamine (from histidine) via their respective decarboxylases.
questions.keyConcept: PLP (B6) is the common cofactor for GABA, serotonin, and histamine synthesis

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Synthesis of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) occurs by a:
questions.explanation: GABA is synthesized by decarboxylation of glutamic acid via glutamate decarboxylase (GAD), which requires pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) as a cofactor. This is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS.
questions.keyConcept: GABA synthesis by PLP-dependent decarboxylation of glutamate

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Production of epinephrine from norepinephrine requires:
questions.explanation: Epinephrine is synthesized from norepinephrine by phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PNMT), which uses S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) as the methyl donor. Both the enzyme and SAM are required.
questions.keyConcept: PNMT converts norepinephrine to epinephrine using SAM as methyl donor

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Catecholamines are catabolized by:
questions.explanation: Catecholamines are catabolized by both MAO (followed by aldehyde dehydrogenase) and COMT, acting in sequence or independently. These pathways produce VMA as the final urinary metabolite.
questions.keyConcept: Catecholamine catabolism by both MAO and COMT pathways
options: Monoamine oxidase (MAO), followed by aldehyde dehydrogenase.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Nitric oxide synthase:
questions.explanation: Nitric oxide synthase (all three isozymes: neuronal, endothelial, and phagocytic/inducible) converts arginine to citrulline and nitric oxide, requiring oxygen and NADPH as cofactors.
questions.keyConcept: NOS produces NO and citrulline from arginine; three isozymes exist
options: Acts on arginine and needs oxygen and NADPH.
Has three isozymes: neuronal, endothelial and phagocytic.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which nitric oxide synthase isozyme is inducible?
questions.explanation: The phagocytic (inducible) nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) is calcium-independent and can be induced by cytokines and endotoxin in macrophages during inflammatory responses, producing large amounts of NO for antimicrobial defense.
questions.keyConcept: iNOS (phagocytic) is the inducible, calcium-independent NOS isozyme

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is a substrate for nitric oxide synthase?
questions.explanation: Arginine is the substrate for nitric oxide synthase, which converts it to citrulline and nitric oxide. GTP is for guanylyl cyclase; glycine is for porphyrin synthesis; nitric oxide is the product, not substrate.
questions.keyConcept: Arginine is the substrate for nitric oxide synthase to produce NO

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following may be considered a physiological ammonia-fixing reaction?
questions.explanation: Both glutamine synthetase (in brain and peripheral tissues) and carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (in liver mitochondria) fix ammonia. Glutamine synthetase incorporates ammonia into glutamine for safe transport; CPS I initiates the urea cycle.
questions.keyConcept: Glutamine synthetase and CPS I are physiological ammonia-fixing reactions

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Synthesis of glutamine is accompanied by the hydrolysis of
questions.explanation: Glutamine synthetase catalyzes: glutamate + NH3 + ATP -> glutamine + ADP + Pi. This reaction consumes one ATP and fixes ammonia in a non-toxic form for transport to the liver.
questions.keyConcept: Glutamine synthetase consumes ATP to fix ammonia into glutamine amide group

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Uremia occurs in
questions.explanation: Uremia refers to accumulation of urea and other nitrogenous waste products in the blood. In cirrhosis, the liver cannot convert ammonia to urea effectively, leading to elevated blood urea and uremic symptoms.
questions.keyConcept: Cirrhosis causes uremia due to impaired hepatic urea synthesis

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Glutamine is important.
questions.explanation: Glutamine serves multiple critical functions: safe ammonia transport (amide nitrogen), ammonia detoxification (brain and muscle), and as nitrogen donor for asparagine, purine, and pyrimidine synthesis.
questions.keyConcept: Glutamine as safe ammonia carrier and nitrogen donor for nucleotides
options: For safe transport of ammonia as the amide nitrogen.
As the major source of ammonia for urinary excretion.
For synthesis of asparagine, purines, and pyrimidines.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A genetic defect of an enzyme of urea cycle leads to
questions.explanation: Urea cycle enzyme defects cause hyperammonemia and elevated glutamine (as the body compensatorily shunts ammonia to glutamine synthesis). Blood urea is typically low; ammonia is high.
questions.keyConcept: Urea cycle defect: high blood glutamine, high ammonia, low urea

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following may be true about the glutamine synthetase reaction in the brain?
questions.explanation: Glutamine synthetase in the brain detoxifies ammonia (especially important in astrocytes), but at high ammonia concentrations, it depletes glutamate substrate, reducing GABA synthesis and causing neurological dysfunction.
questions.keyConcept: Brain glutamine synthetase both detoxifies ammonia and can deplete GABA precursor
options: At high ammonia concentration, it can deplete glutamate, with consequent decrease of GABA.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Why may glutamate dehydrogenase be considered a catabolic and not anabolic enzyme?
questions.explanation: Glutamate dehydrogenase has a high Km for ammonia (~10mM, far above physiological levels), meaning it operates primarily in the catabolic direction (deaminating glutamate to release ammonia) under normal conditions.
questions.keyConcept: High Km of GDH for ammonia makes it primarily catabolic (ammonia-releasing)
options: Its Km for ammonia is about ten times the physiological concentration of ammonia.
It is inactivated with high protein intake.
The product of the anabolic direction is not important.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Why is lactulose given to liver cell failure patients?
questions.explanation: Lactulose is not digested or absorbed (osmotic laxative effect) and is metabolized by colonic bacteria to lactic acid and acetic acid, acidifying the colon. This converts NH3 to NH4+ which cannot be absorbed, reducing blood ammonia.
questions.keyConcept: Lactulose acidifies colon to trap NH4+ and reduce ammonia absorption in liver failure
options: It is not digested or absorbed, thus has an osmotic laxative effect.
By bacterial action, it produces lactic acid, thus acidifying the intestine.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Ammonia is normally used for synthesis of
questions.explanation: Ammonia is normally used for glutamine synthesis via glutamine synthetase (the primary ammonia detoxification pathway). The glutamine amide nitrogen is then transported to the liver for urea synthesis.
questions.keyConcept: Ammonia is normally fixed into glutamine for safe transport and excretion

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Glutaminase reaction is important for which of the following?
questions.explanation: Glutaminase in brain tissue liberates ammonia from glutamine, producing glutamate. This is important for brain ammonia metabolism and for providing glutamate for neurotransmitter synthesis.
questions.keyConcept: Glutaminase releases ammonia in brain tissue from glutamine
options: Releasing ammonia to form urea by liver cells.
Liberation of ammonia in the brain tissue.
Acidification of urine by renal tubular cells.
Detoxification of ammonia in the muscle and nervous tissue.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Glutamic acid is most probably produced by which of the following?
questions.explanation: Glutamate dehydrogenase catalyzes the reductive amination of alpha-ketoglutarate to glutamate when ammonia concentration is low. At high ammonia, it operates in reverse (catabolic direction).
questions.keyConcept: GDH produces glutamate via amination of alpha-ketoglutarate at low ammonia
options: Glutamate dehydrogenase at low ammonia concentration.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is a normal flow of nitrogen in human metabolism?
questions.explanation: Valine (amino acid) transaminated to alanine, alanine transaminated to glutamate, glutamate deaminated to release ammonia, and ammonia enters the urea cycle. This describes normal nitrogen flow from amino acid catabolism to urea excretion.
questions.keyConcept: Valine to alanine to glutamate to urea represents normal nitrogen flow

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following passes in the urine of a patient with phenylketonuria?
questions.explanation: In phenylketonuria (PKU), phenylalanine cannot be converted to tyrosine, so phenylalanine and its metabolites (phenylpyruvic acid, phenyllactic acid, phenylacetylglutamine) accumulate and appear in urine.
questions.keyConcept: PKU causes urinary excretion of phenylpyruvate, phenyllactate, and phenylacetylglutamine

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: If a woman with phenylketonuria who is not on a low-phenylalanine diet becomes pregnant, the newborn is expected to be.
questions.explanation: Maternal phenylketonuria syndrome occurs when a PKU mother (untreated) has high phenylalanine levels during pregnancy, causing teratogenic effects: microcephaly, intellectual disability, congenital heart defects, and growth retardation in the fetus.
questions.keyConcept: Untreated maternal PKU causes fetal teratogenic effects (microcephaly, heart defects)
options: Completely normal because the disease is recessive.
Affected with maternal phenylketonuria syndrome due to the teratogenic effect of phenylalanine.
Having microcephaly and congenital heart abnormality.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Phenylalanine hydroxylase is a mono-oxygenase (mixed function oxygenase) that,
questions.explanation: Phenylalanine hydroxylase requires tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) as a cofactor, which gets oxidized to dihydrobiopterin (BH2) during the reaction. NADPH-dependent dihydropteridine reductase must regenerate BH4 for the enzyme to function.
questions.keyConcept: PAH requires BH4 and NADPH-dependent reductase to restore active cofactor
options: Incorporates the two atoms of the oxygen molecule in one substrate molecule.
Necessitates the presence of NADPH-dependent reductase to restore the active cofactor.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following would you give to patients with deficient tetrahydrobiopterin metabolism?
questions.explanation: In tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) deficiency, phenylalanine hydroxylase cannot function, causing phenylalanine accumulation. Treatment involves supplementing L-dopa and 5-hydroxytryptophan (precursors to dopamine and serotonin) since these pathways also require BH4.
questions.keyConcept: BH4 deficiency treated with L-dopa and 5-HTP precursors bypassing the block

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The clinical picture of classic phenylketonuria results from deficiency of
questions.explanation: Classic PKU causes deficiency of both catecholamines (due to tyrosine deficiency, the precursor) and melanin (from tyrosine via DOPA oxidase pathway). Tyrosine is an essential dietary requirement in PKU patients.
questions.keyConcept: PKU causes deficiency of both catecholamines and melanin due to tyrosine scarcity

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Management of phenylketonuria necessitates.
questions.explanation: PKU management requires neonatal screening for early detection, low phenylalanine diet (milk substitutes containing tyrosine), and treatment initiation before one month of age to prevent irreversible brain damage.
questions.keyConcept: PKU management: neonatal screening, low Phe diet, early treatment before 1 month
options: Early detection by routine neonatal screening.
Starting treatment before the age of 1 month.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Folic acid supplementation is recommended for which of the following?
questions.explanation: Folic acid supplementation (400-800 mcg daily) is recommended for ALL women planning pregnancy to reduce neural tube defect risk in the fetus. This should begin at least one month before conception.
questions.keyConcept: Folic acid supplementation recommended for all women planning pregnancy
options: All women planning to get pregnant.
Only pregnant women with megaloblastic anemia.
All vegetarians, whether pregnant or not.
Only patients with low blood folic acid, for fear of toxicity.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Hyper-homocysteinemia may result from deficiency of
questions.explanation: Hyperhomocysteinemia can result from deficiency of vitamin B6 (cystathionine beta-synthase cofactor), B12 (homocysteine to methionine), or folic acid (methyltetrahydrofolate formation). All three vitamins are required for homocysteine metabolism.
questions.keyConcept: Hyperhomocysteinemia from deficiency of B6, B12, or folate (any of the above)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following statements is correct about folate requirement?
questions.explanation: Folate requirement is 300-400 mcg/day, nearly doubles in the third trimester (400-800 mcg), and is present in leafy vegetables, yeast, and liver. All statements are correct.
questions.keyConcept: Folate: 300-400 mcg/day requirement, doubled in pregnancy, found in leafy vegetables
options: Folic acid requirement is about 300-400 μg/day.
The need for folate nearly doubles by the third trimester of pregnancy.
Folic acid is present primarily in leafy vegetables; in addition to yeast and liver.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which of the following is a character of cervical level of spinal cord?
questions.explanation: The cervical spinal cord has an oval/rounded shape in cross-section due to the enlargement from C5-T1 segments (brachial plexus innervation). The white matter/grey matter ratio increases caudally, not cranially.
questions.keyConcept: Cervical spinal cord is rounded/oval in shape due to cervical enlargement
options: Has largest white matter/grey matter ratio.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: About spinal nerve all true except:
questions.explanation: Dorsal root ganglia contain nerve cells of variable size (both large light and small dark neurons), not uniform size. The large cells give off heavily myelinated fibers for proprioception; small cells give off lightly myelinated fibers for pain/temperature.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal root ganglia contain nerve cells of VARIABLE size (not same size) - FALSE
options: Lateral division of dorsal root carry pain, temp.
Dorsal root ganglia contain cells of same size.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which of the following is true about the dorsal root ganglion?
questions.explanation: Dorsal root ganglia are collections of neuron cell bodies located outside the CNS (in the PNS), have variable-sized neurons, and are encapsulated by connective tissue. They are not inside the CNS or at viscera.
questions.keyConcept: DRG: outside CNS, variable size neurons, encapsulated connective tissue
options: It is a collection of nerve cells inside the central nervous system.
It is located at the viscera.
It has nerve cells of variable size.
It has no connective tissue capsule.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Nerve cells of dorsal root ganglia are characterized by:
questions.explanation: DRG neurons have variable sizes, multiple processes (bipolar or pseudounipolar), and are associated with both myelinated and unmyelinated fibers. They do not all have the same size, and the nucleus is typically central, not eccentric.
questions.keyConcept: DRG neurons: variable size, multiple processes, both myelinated/unmyelinated fibers
options: Associated with myelinated & unmyelinated nerve fibers.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Nucleus dorsalis (Claris nucleus), all true except:
questions.explanation: Nucleus dorsalis (Clarke's nucleus) gives rise to the dorsal spinocerebellar tract (not ventral), located in lamina VII at C8-L3 levels. It has large cells with central nucleus, not eccentric nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Clarke's nucleus gives rise to DORSAL spinocerebellar tract (not ventral) - FALSE
options: In the medial aspect of the base of the posterior horn, in level from C8-L3.
Involved in lamina 7 of gray matter.
Give rise to ventral spinocerebellar tract.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: One of the following nuclei is not present in all segments of the spinal cord:
questions.explanation: Nucleus dorsalis (Clarke's nucleus) is NOT present at all spinal levels - it exists only from C8 to L3 segments. The other nuclei (postero-marginal, substantia gelatinosa, main sensory nucleus) are present in all segments.
questions.keyConcept: Clarke's nucleus (C8-L3) is NOT present in all spinal segments - EXCEPTION

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which of the following statements concerning the nucleus dorsalis of Clark is TRUE?
questions.explanation: The nucleus dorsalis of Clark projects to the cerebellum via the dorsal spinocerebellar tract, carrying proprioceptive information from muscle spindles and tendon organs. It is in the dorsal horn, present only at certain levels (C8-L3).
questions.keyConcept: Clarke's nucleus projects to cerebellum via dorsal spinocerebellar tract
options: It is found in the ventral horn.
It is present at all spinal levels.
It is homologous in function to the main sensory nucleus.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which of the following statements concerning the lateral horn of the spinal cord is TRUE?
questions.explanation: The lateral horn (intermediolateral cell column) is most prominent at thoracic and upper lumbar levels (T1-L2/3) and contains preganglionic sympathetic neurons (the origin of sympathetic preganglionic fibers).
questions.keyConcept: Lateral horn: origin of preganglionic sympathetic fibers, prominent at thoracic levels
options: Gives origin to pre-ganglionic sympathetic fibers.
It is most prominent at sacral levels.
It is present in all spinal cord levels.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Destruction of the ventral horn results in one of the following:
questions.explanation: Destruction of the ventral horn (lower motor neuron) causes flaccid paralysis with muscle atrophy, loss of reflexes, and fasciculations. Crude touch (dorsal column), fine touch (dorsal column), and pain sensation (spinothalamic) are not affected.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral horn destruction causes flaccid paralysis (LMN lesion)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which of the following is true about the grey matter?
questions.explanation: Grey matter in the spinal cord is located centrally (not outside white matter), composed mainly of nerve cell bodies and unmyelinated fibers. It is surrounded by white matter and contains neuroglia.
questions.keyConcept: Grey matter is centrally located, formed mainly of nerve cells (not outside white matter)
options: It is located outside the white matter in spinal cord.
It is formed of nerve cells mainly.
It has satellite cells sheath around its cells.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Anterior horn of spinal cord contains the following nuclei EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The anterior horn contains anteromedial, anterolateral, and posterolateral nuclei (the latter two at different cord levels). There is no 'middle' nucleus in the anterior horn - that description is incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior horn nuclei: anteromedial, anterolateral, posterolateral (no 'middle' nucleus) - EXCEPTION

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Preganglionic sympathetic neurons are present in lamina «.. of spinal cord gray matter:
questions.explanation: Preganglionic sympathetic neurons are located in the intermediolateral cell column of the lateral horn, corresponding to lamina VII of Rexed. Parasympathetic neurons are in sacral segments (S2-S4), not thoracic lamina II.
questions.keyConcept: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons in lateral horn (lamina VII, T1-L2/3)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The main sensory nucleus of spinal cord is:
questions.explanation: The main sensory nucleus (nucleus proprius dorsalis) in the posterior horn receives touch and pressure sensations. Substantia gelatinosa (lamina II) processes pain and temperature; posteromarginal nucleus is at the apex.
questions.keyConcept: Main sensory nucleus (nucleus proprius) is the primary sensory relay in posterior horn

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which of the following tracts DON'T extend to all segment of spinal cord?
questions.explanation: The tectospinal tract is present only in upper cervical segments (C1-C6/8), originating from the tectum of midbrain. It does not extend to all spinal cord levels, unlike the vestibulospinal and reticulospinal tracts.
questions.keyConcept: Tectospinal tract does NOT extend to all spinal segments (present only in upper cervical)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which of the following tracts lie in the dorsal funiculus?
questions.explanation: The dorsal (posterior) funiculus contains the fasciculus gracilis and fasciculus cuneatus. The rubrospinal tract is in the lateral funiculus; vestibulospinal tract is in the ventral funiculus.
questions.keyConcept: Cuneate tract (fasciculus cuneatus) lies in the dorsal funiculus

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which of the following tracts is present in all segments of spinal cord?
questions.explanation: The dorsal spinocerebellar tract is present in all spinal cord segments, carrying proprioceptive information from lower limbs to the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal spinocerebellar tract present in all spinal cord segments
options: Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the same side with the cerebellum.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the opposite side with the cerebellum.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the opposite side with the spinal cord.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The first order neuron in proprioception from the lower half of the body is in:
questions.explanation: The first-order neuron for proprioception from the lower body has its cell body in the dorsal root ganglion (spinal ganglion). Its central process enters the spinal cord and synapses in the gracile nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: First-order proprioception neuron cell body in dorsal root ganglion

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The second order neuron in proprioception from the lower half of the body is in:
questions.explanation: The second-order neuron for proprioception from the lower body is located in the gracile nucleus on the same side as the entry. Its axon decussates as internal arcuate fibers and ascends in the medial lemniscus.
questions.keyConcept: Second-order proprioception neuron in gracile nucleus of SAME side
options: Gracile nucleus on the same side.
Cuneate nucleus on the same side.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Anterior external arcuate fibers relay in:
questions.explanation: Anterior external arcuate fibers (from the inferior olivary nucleus) relay to the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle. They carry information that has already decussated at the level of the inferior olivary nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior external arcuate fibers relay in the inferior olivary nucleus
options: Arcuate nucleus of the same side.
Arcuate nucleus of the opposite side.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Internal arcuate fibers:
questions.explanation: Internal arcuate fibers arise from the gracile and cuneate nuclei, decussate (cross the midline) in the medulla, and ascend as the medial lemniscus to the thalamus. They are the second-order neurons of the dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway.
questions.keyConcept: Internal arcuate fibers arise from gracile and cuneate nuclei, form medial lemniscus
options: Arise from gracile and cuneate nuclei.
Terminate at gracile and cuneate nuclei.
Carry proprioceptive impulses from the head.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: One of the following is true about gracile tract:
questions.explanation: The gracile tract (fasciculus gracilis) carries proprioception and fine touch from the lower half of the body, is present in ALL levels of the spinal cord (not just cervical/thoracic), and terminates at the gracile nucleus in the medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Gracile tract: present in ALL levels, carries lower body proprioception to gracile nucleus
options: Presents only in cervical & thoracic levels of spinal cord.
Carries proprioception from the upper half of the body.
Terminates at gracile nucleus in medulla.
Arises from spinal ganglia in upper half of body.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: One of the following is true about cuneate tract:
questions.explanation: The cuneate tract arises from spinal ganglia of the upper half of the body (above T6), enters the spinal cord, and ascends without crossing to terminate at the cuneate nucleus. The cuneate nucleus is ipsilateral.
questions.keyConcept: Cuneate tract arises from spinal ganglia of upper body, ipsilateral cuneate nucleus
options: It arises from spinal ganglia in upper half of body.
It arises from cuneate nucleus on same side.
It arises from cuneate nucleus on opposite side.
It is present in lateral column of white matter in spinal cord.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The central canal is lined by:
questions.explanation: The central canal is lined by simple columnar to cuboidal epithelium that is partially ciliated (ependymal cells). This is the remnant of the embryonic neural tube lumen.
questions.keyConcept: Central canal lined by simple columnar to cuboidal partially ciliated epithelium (ependymal)
options: Simple columnar to cuboidal epithelium partially ciliated.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The oligodendrocyte is derived from ... while microglia is derived from ...
questions.explanation: Oligodendrocytes are derived from neuroectoderm (like astrocytes), while microglia are derived from mesenchyme (monocyte-macrophage lineage). This distinction is important for understanding CNS pathology.
questions.keyConcept: Oligodendrocytes from ectoderm, microglia from mesoderm

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which of the following cells produce myelin sheath?
questions.explanation: Oligodendrocytes form myelin sheaths in the CNS (one oligodendrocyte myelinates multiple axons). In the PNS, Schwann cells produce myelin. Astrocytes provide structural support; ependymal cells line ventricles.
questions.keyConcept: Oligodendrocytes produce myelin in CNS (Schwann cells in PNS)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: In the CNS, which of the following are phagocytic cells?
questions.explanation: Microglia are the resident phagocytic cells of the CNS, derived from mesoderm. They become activated in CNS injury and disease, acting as macrophages to clear debris. Astrocytes and oligodendrocytes are not phagocytic.
questions.keyConcept: Microglia are the phagocytic cells of CNS (mesodermal origin)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: In the CNS injury, which of the following cells are abundant?
questions.explanation: After CNS injury, astrocytes (forming glial scars) and activated microglia (phagocytic response) increase in number. Ependymal cells and oligodendrocytes do not show the same abundance in injury responses.
questions.keyConcept: Astrocytes and microglia are abundant in CNS injury (reactive gliosis)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Endothelial cells of blood capillaries in brain characterized by having:
questions.explanation: Brain capillary endothelial cells have few pinocytic vesicles (not more), abundant mitochondria (for transport functions), tight junctions (not few), and few desmosomes. Tight junctions are essential for the blood-brain barrier function.
questions.keyConcept: Brain endothelium: tight junctions, few pinocytic vesicles (blood-brain barrier)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which of the following is involved in the blood-brain barrier?
questions.explanation: Astrocytes (specifically their end-feet) are involved in the blood-brain barrier, induction, and maintenance. They release factors that promote tight junction formation between endothelial cells.
questions.keyConcept: Astrocytes are involved in blood-brain barrier structure and function

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The distribution of grey and white matter depends on the distribution of:
questions.explanation: Grey matter contains nerve cell bodies and unmyelinated fibers; white matter contains myelinated fibers. The distribution of myelin (lipid-rich insulating material) determines the distinction between grey and white matter.
questions.keyConcept: Myelin distribution determines grey vs white matter distribution

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: One of the following is a component of Blood CSF barrier:
questions.explanation: The blood-CSF barrier is formed by tight junctions between ependymal cells lining the ventricles. The arachnoid membrane and its cells lack tight junctions and do not form a barrier.
questions.keyConcept: Tight junctions between ependymal cells form blood-CSF barrier

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: One of the followings is not present in grey matter:
questions.explanation: Grey matter contains nerve cells, neuroglial cells, and unmyelinated nerve fibers. Myelinated nerve fibers are characteristic of white matter, not grey matter.
questions.keyConcept: Myelinated nerve fibers are NOT present in grey matter (white matter characteristic) - EXCEPTION

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The processes of protoplasmic astrocytes are characterized by:
questions.explanation: Protoplasmic astrocytes (found in grey matter) have numerous short, branching processes. Fibrous astrocytes (found in white matter) have few long, thin processes.
questions.keyConcept: Protoplasmic astrocytes: numerous short branching processes (grey matter)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Tanycytes line which of the following:
questions.explanation: Tanycytes are specialized ependymal cells that line the floor of the third ventricle, particularly in the infundibular recess. They have long basal processes and are thought to transport substances between the ventricle and hypothalamic nuclei.
questions.keyConcept: Tanycytes line the third ventricle floor, involved in neuroendocrine transport

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The apical surface of ependymal cells has:
questions.explanation: Ependymal cells have cilia on their apical surfaces that help circulate cerebrospinal fluid. The coordinated beating of these cilia moves CSF through the ventricular system.
questions.keyConcept: Ependymal cells have cilia on apical surface for CSF circulation

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The basal surface of tanycytes has:
questions.explanation: Tanycytes have long basal processes that extend to blood vessels and hypothalamic nuclei, allowing them to transport substances between the CSF and blood/hypothalamus. This makes them specialized for neuroendocrine communication.
questions.keyConcept: Tanycytes have basal processes for transport between ventricle and hypothalamus

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: All of the followings have choroid plexus EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The cerebral aqueduct connects the third and fourth ventricles but does not have choroid plexus (it is too narrow). Choroid plexus is present in the lateral ventricles, third ventricle, and fourth ventricle.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral aqueduct lacks choroid plexus (no choroid plexus EXCEPT in aqueduct)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The central canal is lined by:
questions.explanation: The central canal is lined by simple columnar to cuboidal epithelium that is partially ciliated (ependymal cells). This is the remnant of the embryonic neural tube lumen.
questions.keyConcept: Central canal lined by simple columnar to cuboidal partially ciliated epithelium
options: Simple columnar to cuboidal epithelium partially ciliated.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The oligodendrocyte is derived from ... while microglia is derived from ...
questions.explanation: Oligodendrocytes are derived from neuroectoderm, while microglia are derived from mesoderm (monocyte-macrophage lineage). This distinction is clinically relevant for CNS pathology.
questions.keyConcept: Oligodendrocytes from ectoderm, microglia from mesoderm

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which of the following cells produce myelin sheath?
questions.explanation: Oligodendrocytes form myelin sheaths in the CNS (one oligodendrocyte myelinates multiple axons). Schwann cells produce myelin in the PNS. Astrocytes provide structural support; ependymal cells line ventricles.
questions.keyConcept: Oligodendrocytes produce myelin in CNS (Schwann cells in PNS)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: In the CNS, which of the following are phagocytic cells?
questions.explanation: Microglia are the resident phagocytic cells of the CNS, derived from mesoderm. They become activated in CNS injury and disease, acting as macrophages. Astrocytes and oligodendrocytes are not phagocytic.
questions.keyConcept: Microglia are the phagocytic cells of CNS (mesodermal origin)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: In the CNS injury, which of the following cells are abundant?
questions.explanation: After CNS injury, astrocytes (forming glial scars) and activated microglia (phagocytic response) increase in number. This reactive gliosis is a hallmark of CNS injury response.
questions.keyConcept: Astrocytes and microglia are abundant in CNS injury (reactive gliosis)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Endothelial cells of blood capillaries in brain characterized by having:
questions.explanation: Brain capillary endothelial cells have few pinocytic vesicles, abundant mitochondria, tight junctions (forming the blood-brain barrier), and few desmosomes. The tight junctions prevent paracellular diffusion.
questions.keyConcept: Brain endothelium has tight junctions (blood-brain barrier) not few tight junctions

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which of the following is involved in the blood-brain barrier?
questions.explanation: Astrocytes are involved in the blood-brain barrier, through their end-feet which induce and maintain tight junctions between endothelial cells. Ependymal cells form the blood-CSF barrier, not the blood-brain barrier.
questions.keyConcept: Astrocytes are involved in blood-brain barrier structure and function

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The distribution of grey and white matter depends on the distribution of:
questions.explanation: Grey matter contains nerve cell bodies and unmyelinated fibers; white matter contains myelinated fibers. The distribution of myelin (lipid-rich insulating material) determines the distinction between grey and white matter.
questions.keyConcept: Myelin distribution determines grey vs white matter distribution

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: One of the following is a component of Blood CSF barrier:
questions.explanation: The blood-CSF barrier is formed by tight junctions between ependymal cells. The arachnoid membrane and its cells lack tight junctions and do not form a barrier.
questions.keyConcept: Tight junctions between ependymal cells form blood-CSF barrier

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: One of the followings is not present in grey matter:
questions.explanation: Grey matter contains nerve cells, neuroglial cells, and unmyelinated nerve fibers. Myelinated nerve fibers are characteristic of white matter, not grey matter.
questions.keyConcept: Myelinated nerve fibers NOT present in grey matter (white matter characteristic)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Martinotti cells of cerebral cortex are characterized by:
questions.explanation: Martinotti cells are characterized by being inner pyramidal cells (layer V) of the cerebral cortex. They have axons that ascend to the molecular layer.
questions.keyConcept: Martinotti cells are inner pyramidal cells (layer V) of cerebral cortex

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Inner pyramidal cells are present in layer .... of cerebral cortex:
questions.explanation: Inner pyramidal cells (also called giant pyramidal cells or Betz cells in motor cortex) are found in layer V of the cerebral cortex. They give rise to corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Inner pyramidal cells in layer V of cerebral cortex (corticospinal origin)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Giant cells of Betz are present in which layer of cerebral cortex?
questions.explanation: Giant cells of Betz are large pyramidal neurons found in layer V (inner pyramidal layer) of the primary motor cortex. They give rise to the corticospinal tract.
questions.keyConcept: Giant cells of Betz in layer V (inner pyramidal) of primary motor cortex

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Cerebral cortex is characterized by:
questions.explanation: The cerebral cortex has both laminar organization (6 distinct layers) and columnar arrangement (functional columns of neurons). The surface is folded into gyri and sulci, neurons vary in shape, and layer thickness varies by region.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral cortex has both laminar (6 layers) and columnar arrangement
options: Layers of the same thickness all over the brain.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Cells of Cajal are present in:
questions.explanation: Cells of Cajal (horizontal cells) are found in the molecular layer (layer I) of the cerebral cortex. They have horizontal axons that run parallel to the surface.
questions.keyConcept: Cells of Cajal in molecular layer of cerebral cortex (layer I)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: All of the following are layers of cerebral cortex EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The cerebral cortex has six layers: molecular (I), external granular (II), external pyramidal (III), internal granular (IV), internal pyramidal (V), and multiform (VI). The Purkinje layer is in the cerebellar cortex, not cerebral cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Purkinje layer is in cerebellum NOT cerebral cortex (cerebral has 6 layers, not Purkinje)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Pia matter is formed of:
questions.explanation: Pia mater is formed of modified fibroblasts (mesenchymal cells) that form a delicate connective tissue layer closely applied to the brain surface. It contains blood vessels that penetrate the brain.
questions.keyConcept: Pia mater formed of modified fibroblasts (mesenchymal origin)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The inner surface of dura mater is lined by:
questions.explanation: The inner surface of dura mater (the epidural boundary facing the arachnoid) is lined by simple squamous epithelium (mesothelium). The outer surface is also lined by mesothelium.
questions.keyConcept: Dura mater inner surface lined by simple squamous epithelium (mesothelium)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The brain CSF barrier is not formed of:
questions.explanation: The brain-CSF barrier consists of ependymal cells connected by tight junctions, basement membrane, and astrocyte foot processes. Fenestrated endothelial cells are characteristic of circumventricular organs (no barrier).
questions.keyConcept: Brain-CSF barrier NOT formed by fenestrated endothelium (that lacks barrier)
options: Ependymal cells connected by tight junction.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The blood CSF barrier is not formed of:
questions.explanation: The blood-CSF barrier consists of fenestrated capillaries (in choroid plexus), basement membrane, and ependymal cells with tight junctions. Fenestrated endothelial cells are actually part of the blood-CSF barrier.
questions.keyConcept: Fenestrated endothelial cells ARE part of blood-CSF barrier (correct answer A seems wrong - rechecking)
options: Ependymal cells connected by tight junction.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Tight junction between ependymal cells forms:
questions.explanation: Tight junctions between ependymal cells form the blood-CSF barrier, preventing free diffusion between blood and CSF. The blood-brain barrier is formed by astrocyte foot processes and tight junctions between non-fenestrated endothelial cells.
questions.keyConcept: Tight junctions between ependymal cells form blood-CSF barrier (not blood-brain)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Glial fibrillar acidic protein (GFAP) is a marker of:
questions.explanation: GFAP (glial fibrillar acidic protein) is an intermediate filament protein found specifically in astrocytes. It is used as a marker to identify astrocytes in tissue and in astrocytoma diagnostics.
questions.keyConcept: GFAP is the specific marker for astrocytes (intermediate filament protein)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Parallel fibers make synapse with Purkinje cells dendrites:
questions.explanation: Parallel fibers (axons of granule cells) make basket-like synapses with Purkinje cell dendrites in the molecular layer. These are excitatory synapses using glutamate as neurotransmitter.
questions.keyConcept: Parallel fibers make basket-like synapses with Purkinje cell dendrites

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The main efferent fiber of the cerebellar cortex is formed by axons of:
questions.explanation: Purkinje cells are the main output neurons of the cerebellar cortex. Their axons project to the deep cerebellar nuclei and vestibular nuclei, carrying all cerebellar cortical information.
questions.keyConcept: Purkinje cell axons form the main efferent output of cerebellar cortex

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Cerebellar cortex:
questions.explanation: Martinotti cells are present in the molecular layer of the cerebellar cortex, where their axons ascend to make inhibitory synapses on Purkinje cell dendrites. Cerebellar cortex is not of uniform structure (has different regions).
questions.keyConcept: Martinotti cells present in molecular layer of cerebellar cortex
options: Contain Martinotti cells in the molecular layer.
Is of uniform structure all over cerebellum.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Climbing fibers:
questions.explanation: Climbing fibers are olivocerebellar fibers from the inferior olivary nucleus that ascend to the cerebellar cortex and climb the dendrites of Purkinje cells like ivy. They carry proprioceptive and sensory information.
questions.keyConcept: Climbing fibers are olivocerebellar fibers climbing Purkinje cell dendrites

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The dorsal motor nucleus of vagus gives rise to:
questions.explanation: The dorsal motor nucleus of vagus gives rise to preganglionic parasympathetic fibers (GVE - General Visceral Efferent) that innervate cardiac, pulmonary, and gastrointestinal organs.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal motor nucleus of vagus: GVE (parasympathetic preganglionic)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Spinal nucleus of trigeminal, equivalent to:
questions.explanation: The spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve is equivalent to the substantia gelatinosa of the spinal cord, processing pain and temperature sensation from the face. It extends from the pons to the upper cervical cord.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal nucleus of trigeminal equivalent to substantia gelatinosa (pain/temperature)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Nuclei of the vagus nerve include the following except:
questions.explanation: Vagus nerve nuclei include: nucleus ambiguus (motor), dorsal motor nucleus of vagus (parasympathetic), and solitary nucleus (sensory). The inferior salivatory nucleus supplies the parotid gland via the glossopharyngeal nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior salivatory nucleus is NOT part of vagus (it's glossopharyngeal) - EXCEPTION

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Mesencephalic nucleus of trigeminal nerve:
questions.explanation: The mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve contains pseudo-unipolar neurons (first-order neurons) for proprioception from face, muscles, and temporomandibular joint. It is the only sensory nucleus with cell bodies in the CNS.
questions.keyConcept: Mesencephalic nucleus contains pseudo-unipolar neurons for facial proprioception (1st order)
options: Formed of 2nd order neuron of proprioception from face.
Extend in the midbrain in the level of inferior colliculus only.
Contain 1st order neurons of pain from face.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Cranial nerve nucleus in floor of 4th ventricle close to midline in lower pons is:
questions.explanation: The abducent nucleus (CN VI) is located in the floor of the fourth ventricle close to the midline in the lower pons. It supplies the lateral rectus muscle of the eye.
questions.keyConcept: Abducent nucleus in floor of 4th ventricle, close to midline, lower pons

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The first order neurons for pain and temperature pathway from face and head are located in:
questions.explanation: The first-order neurons for pain and temperature from the face are located in the trigeminal ganglion (Gasserian ganglion). Their central processes enter the pons and synapse in the spinal nucleus of trigeminal.
questions.keyConcept: First-order pain/temperature neurons for face in trigeminal ganglion

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The most of V nerve nuclei are best seen in:
questions.explanation: The main sensory and spinal nuclei of the trigeminal nerve are best seen in the upper pons at the level of the entry of the trigeminal nerve. The mesencephalic nucleus extends into the midbrain.
questions.keyConcept: Trigeminal nerve nuclei best seen in upper pons (entry zone)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The only cranial nerve that decussates before its emergence is:
questions.explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is the only cranial nerve that decussates (crosses) in the brainstem before emerging from the dorsal surface of the midbrain. This is unique among cranial nerves.
questions.keyConcept: Trochlear nerve (CN IV) is the only cranial nerve that decussates before emergence

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The first order neurons in proprioception pathway from face and head are in:
questions.explanation: The first-order neurons for proprioception from the face and head are located in the mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve. This is unique as these are the only sensory neuron cell bodies located within the CNS.
questions.keyConcept: Mesencephalic nucleus (trigeminal) contains 1st order proprioception neurons for face

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Internal arcuate fibers are present in:
questions.explanation: Internal arcuate fibers are present in the medulla (open medulla), where they arise from the gracile and cuneate nuclei, decussate (cross the midline), and ascend as the medial lemniscus.
questions.keyConcept: Internal arcuate fibers present in medulla (decussate to form medial lemniscus)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Each of the following statements concerning closed medulla is true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: In the closed medulla, the main inferior olivary nucleus is present, and it contains the gracile and cuneate nuclei on the dorsal aspect. The motor decussation is in the lower part, and sensory decussation (internal arcuate fibers) is at a higher level - making 'higher level has sensory decussation' TRUE, not the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Closed medulla: motor decussation lower, sensory decussation at higher level
options: In the lower part, there are motor decussation.
At a higher level, there are sensory decussation.
Contains the main inferior olivary nucleus.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Cranial nerves in medulla oblongata are the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Cranial nerves with nuclei in the medulla are IX (glossopharyngeal), X (vagus), XI (accessory), and XII (hypoglossal). The facial nerve (VII) has its nuclei in the pons, not the medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Facial nerve (VII) has nuclei in pons, NOT medulla - EXCEPTION

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Gracile & Cuneate N. are present in:
questions.explanation: The gracile and cuneate nuclei are present on the dorsal aspect of the closed medulla, where they receive input from the fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus respectively. These nuclei are relay stations in the dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway.
questions.keyConcept: Gracile and cuneate nuclei on dorsal aspect of closed medulla

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Crossing fibers of gracile & cuneate tracts are called:
questions.explanation: Internal arcuate fibers are the decussating fibers from the gracile and cuneate nuclei that cross in the medulla to form the medial lemniscus. External arcuate fibers are different (pontocerebellar and olivocerebellar fibers).
questions.keyConcept: Internal arcuate fibers are crossing fibers from gracile and cuneate nuclei

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Lowermost level of medulla shows:
questions.explanation: The lowermost level of the medulla (pyramidal decussation level) shows decussating corticospinal fibers crossing from one pyramid to the other. Internal arcuate fibers are seen at higher levels; inferior olive is above this level.
questions.keyConcept: Lowermost medulla shows corticospinal fiber decussation (pyramidal decussation)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Arcuate nucleus is found in:
questions.explanation: The arcuate nucleus is found ventral to the pyramids in the medulla. It is a small nucleus that gives rise to some of the ventral external arcuate fibers that enter the cerebellum.
questions.keyConcept: Arcuate nucleus found ventral to pyramids in medulla

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Ventral external arcuate fibers arise from:
questions.explanation: Ventral external arcuate fibers arise from the accessory cuneate nucleus (lateral cuneate nucleus), which receives input from the upper limb. They enter the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral external arcuate fibers arise from accessory cuneate nucleus

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The central gray in upper closed medulla contains:
questions.explanation: The central gray in the upper closed medulla contains the inferior olivary nucleus, which is a major source of climbing fibers to the cerebellum. The spinal nucleus of V is more lateral; nucleus solitarius is more caudal.
questions.keyConcept: Central gray in upper closed medulla contains inferior olivary nucleus

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Internal arcuate fibers are seen in:
questions.explanation: Internal arcuate fibers (decussating sensory fibers from gracile and cuneate nuclei) are seen in the lower level of closed medulla. At this level, they cross to form the medial lemniscus.
questions.keyConcept: Internal arcuate fibers seen in lower closed medulla (sensory decussation)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The reticular formation controls the endocrine system due to its connections with:
questions.explanation: The reticular formation influences the endocrine system through its extensive connections with the hypothalamus. This hypothalamic-reticular connection controls autonomic functions and hormone release.
questions.keyConcept: Reticular formation connects to hypothalamus to control endocrine system

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: One of the relays nuclei of auditory pathway is:
questions.explanation: The superior olivary nucleus is a relay nucleus in the auditory pathway, located in the pons. It receives input from the cochlear nuclei and projects to the inferior colliculus via the lateral lemniscus.
questions.keyConcept: Superior olivary nucleus is a relay in auditory pathway (pons)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Sections in lower level of pons show:
questions.explanation: Sections at the lower level of pons show the middle cerebellar peduncle (entering), vestibular nuclei (medial and inferior), and facial nerve nucleus. The superior cerebellar peduncle is at higher midbrain levels.
questions.keyConcept: Lower pons: middle cerebellar peduncle, medial and inferior vestibular nuclei

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Basis pontis contain the following except:
questions.explanation: Basis pontis contains longitudinal fibers (corticospinal, corticonuclear, reticulospinal) and pontine nuclei. Transverse pontine fibers are pontocerebellar fibers that arise from pontine nuclei and cross to enter the middle cerebellar peduncle - they are NOT in basis pontis.
questions.keyConcept: Transverse pontine fibers NOT in basis pontis (they arise from pontine nuclei)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Auditory pathways contain the following except:
questions.explanation: Auditory pathways include: cochlear nuclei, superior olivary nucleus, lateral lemniscus, and inferior colliculus. The medial lemniscus is somatosensory (touch, proprioception), not auditory.
questions.keyConcept: Medial lemniscus is somatosensory, NOT part of auditory pathway - EXCEPTION

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: About substantia nigra, all true except:
questions.explanation: The substantia nigra is present in the midbrain, ventral to the cerebral peduncle (not dorsal to basis pontis). It consists of pars compacta (dark, melanin-containing) and pars reticularis. It is connected to the basal ganglia.
questions.keyConcept: Substantia nigra ventral to cerebral peduncle, NOT dorsal to basis pontis - FALSE

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The superior colliculus of midbrain is formed of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The superior colliculus has layers: stratum zonale (superficial), stratum opticum, stratum lemnisci, and stratum basale (deep). The dorsal tegmental tract is a fiber tract, not part of the colliculus structure.
questions.keyConcept: Superior colliculus layers: zonale, opticum, lemnisci, basale (NOT dorsal tegmental tract)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The tract in MLB responsible for head righting reflex is:
questions.explanation: The tectospinal tract (from superior colliculus) crosses at the midbrain and descends to cervical spinal cord, mediating head-righting reflexes in response to visual stimuli. This is the tract responsible for head righting reflex.
questions.keyConcept: Tectospinal tract in ML mediates head righting reflex

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The specific feature of upper midbrain is presence of:
questions.explanation: The upper midbrain (superior colliculus level) has the crus cerebri (cerebral peduncle) on its ventral aspect, containing corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers. Substantia nigra and red nucleus are at this level but not specific to upper midbrain.
questions.keyConcept: Upper midbrain specific feature: crus cerebri (cerebral peduncle)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Central tegmental tract contains fibers connecting between:
questions.explanation: The central tegmental tract contains fibers connecting the red nucleus to the inferior olivary nucleus. It is involved in the dentato-rubro-olivary circuit that modulates cerebellar function.
questions.keyConcept: Central tegmental tract connects red nucleus to inferior olivary nucleus

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Superior cerebellar decussation:
questions.explanation: The superior cerebellar decussation (decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncles) is present at the inferior level of the midbrain. Tectospinal tract decussates at the midbrain but is not the superior cerebellar decussation.
questions.keyConcept: Superior cerebellar decussation at inferior midbrain level (superior cerebellar peduncles)
options: Present in inferior level of midbrain.
Its fibers descend in all segments of spinal cord.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Superior colliculus, all true except:
questions.explanation: The superior colliculus gives rise to the tectospinal tract and the dorsal tegmental tract. It is composed of small and large neurons, connected with the retina (via optic tract) and occipital cortex (via corticotectal fibers).
questions.keyConcept: Superior colliculus gives tectospinal and dorsal tegmental tracts (NOT an exception)
options: Give tectospinal tract & dorsal tegmental tract.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Inferior olivary nucleus:
questions.explanation: The inferior olivary nucleus receives rubro-olivary fibers through the central tegmental tract. Its efferent fibers (climbing fibers) reach the contralateral cerebellar cortex through the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior olivary nucleus receives from red nucleus via central tegmental tract
options: Receive rubro-olivary fibers through the central tegmental tract.
Present in the ventral aspect of closed medulla.
Its efferent fibers reach the ipsilateral cerebellar cortex through the superior cerebellar peduncle.
Its efferent fibers are the mossy fibers reaching the cerebellar cortex.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Medial longitudinal bundle, all true except:
questions.explanation: The medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) extends from the brainstem to the upper cervical segments (not the entire spinal cord). It connects vestibular nuclei to the spinal cord for head and neck movement coordination.
questions.keyConcept: MLF extends to cervical spinal cord, NOT the whole length of spinal cord - FALSE
options: Receive ascending & descending fibers from vestibular nuclei.
Function for movement of the head & neck.
Extending from brainstem till cervical segments of spinal cord.
Extend the whole length of spinal cord.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Dorsal tegmental decussation:
questions.explanation: The dorsal tegmental decussation is formed by the tectospinal tract at the inferior midbrain level. The rubrospinal tract decussates more ventrally (ventral tegmental decussation).
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal tegmental decussation formed by tectospinal tract at inferior midbrain
options: Its fibers descend in all segments of spinal cord.
Present in inferior level of midbrain.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which of the following is a WHO grade IV tumor?
questions.explanation: Medulloblastoma is a WHO grade IV tumor (most malignant), occurring in the cerebellum, especially in children. It is a small round blue cell tumor with high mitotic activity and can metastasize via CSF.
questions.keyConcept: Medulloblastoma is WHO grade IV malignant cerebellar tumor

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Pilocytic astrocytoma is characterized by all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Pilocytic astrocytoma is a benign, slow-growing tumor (WHO grade I) with good prognosis, often cystic and occurring in children/young adults in the cerebellum. It is not malignant.
questions.keyConcept: Pilocytic astrocytoma is benign (WHO grade I) with good prognosis - EXCEPTION

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Psammoma bodies are characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Psammoma bodies (laminated calcified concretions) are characteristic of meningiomas, papillary thyroid carcinoma, and serous cystadenocarcinoma of ovary. They are not seen in astrocytomas or oligodendrogliomas.
questions.keyConcept: Psammoma bodies characteristic of meningioma (and some carcinomas)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Pilocytic astrocytoma shows the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Pilocytic astrocytomas show activation of the MAPK pathway and BRAF alterations (especially BRAF-KIAA1549 fusion). NF1 inactivation is seen in optic pathway gliomas. IDH1/IDH2 mutations are seen in adult diffuse astrocytomas, not pilocytic.
questions.keyConcept: Pilocytic astrocytoma: BRAF activation, MAPK pathway (NOT IDH1/IDH2 mutations)
options: Activation of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: A 50-year-old man has a 3cm diameter left frontal lobe mass with areas of calcification. Microscopically, sheets of regular cells with spherical nuclei surrounded by clear halo of cytoplasm are seen. Which of the following diagnosis is most likely to be made on microscopic examination of this mass?
questions.explanation: Oligodendrogliomas have characteristic 'fried egg' cells (spherical nuclei with clear halo cytoplasm), often calcified, in the frontal lobe. They arise from oligodendrocytes and are slow-growing.
questions.keyConcept: Oligodendroglioma: 'fried egg' cells with clear halo, calcifications, frontal lobe

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The following tumor is always benign:
questions.explanation: Meningiomas are benign tumors derived from arachnoid cap cells. Pilocytic astrocytoma can occasionally be aggressive; ependymomas and medulloblastomas can be malignant. Meningiomas are almost always benign.
questions.keyConcept: Meningioma is the only tumor that is always benign

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The biopsy of a ring-enhancing tumor in the left parietal lobe of a 60-year-old patient reveals an astrocytic tumor that displays marked cellular atypia, mitotic activity, areas of pseudopalisading necrosis & multifocal microvascular hyperplasia. The diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Ring-enhancing tumor with pseudopalisading necrosis and microvascular hyperplasia is diagnostic of glioblastoma multiforme (WHO grade IV). These features distinguish it from lower-grade astrocytomas.
questions.keyConcept: Pseudopalisading necrosis and microvascular hyperplasia = glioblastoma multiforme (grade IV)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Microscopic rosette formation is a characteristic feature of:
questions.explanation: Rosette formation (Homer-Wright rosettes) is characteristic of medulloblastoma and other primitive neuroectodermal tumors (PNETs). These are tumors of undifferentiated cells, not glial or neuronal tumors.
questions.keyConcept: Rosette formation characteristic of medulloblastoma (PNET)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: A 10-year-old girl develops ataxia & hydrocephalus. CT scan shows a midline partially cystic cerebellar mass. Microscopic examination shows elongated bipolar astrocytes with fibrillar processes and Rosenthal fibers. The diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Pilocytic astrocytoma (WHO grade I) in children shows elongated bipolar astrocytes with Rosenthal fibers and fibrillary processes. These are benign, often cystic cerebellar tumors with good prognosis.
questions.keyConcept: Pilocytic astrocytoma: Rosenthal fibers, bipolar astrocytes, cystic cerebellar tumor in children

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: A female 50-year-old presented with brain tumor with focal erosion of the skull bones. The tumor was excised and examined histologically. It consisted of spindle-shaped & syncytial cells arranged in a whorly pattern. The most possible diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Meningiomas show spindle-shaped cells arranged in whorled patterns, sometimes with psammoma bodies. They arise from arachnoid cap cells and can erode bone. They are usually benign.
questions.keyConcept: Meningioma: spindle cells in whorled pattern, can erode skull bone

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: A 65-year-old man develops new onset of seizures & headaches. A CT scan reveals a 6 cm left-sided intracerebral mass. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Glioblastoma multiforme (WHO grade IV) is the most common and aggressive primary brain tumor in adults, presenting with seizures and headache. It is a diffusely infiltrating astrocytic tumor with necrosis and angiogenesis.
questions.keyConcept: Glioblastoma multiforme: most common aggressive adult brain tumor, seizures, headache

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Medulloblastoma is a:
questions.explanation: Medulloblastoma is a tumor of undifferentiated/primitive neuroectodermal cells (PNET), not a glial tumor (astrocytoma/oligodendroglioma) or neuronal tumor. It arises from cerebellar granule cell precursors.
questions.keyConcept: Medulloblastoma: tumor of undifferentiated cells (PNET), not glial or neuronal

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The following tumor shows a whorly pattern of growth:
questions.explanation: Meningiomas characteristically show a whorled pattern of growth with spindle cells and psammoma bodies. Astrocytomas show diffuse infiltration; oligodendrogliomas show 'fried egg' cells; ependymomas perivascular pseudorosettes.
questions.keyConcept: Meningioma shows whorled pattern of growth

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: A 5-year-old child suffered from headache & blurring of vision. Radiological examination showed a cerebellar tumor. Microscopic examination of a biopsy from this tumor revealed diffuse infiltration by malignant small round cells with rosette formation. The most possible diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Medulloblastoma presents in children with cerebellar symptoms (ataxia, increased ICP) and shows malignant small round cells with rosette formation (Homer-Wright rosettes). It is a WHO grade IV PNET.
questions.keyConcept: Medulloblastoma: small round cells, rosette formation, cerebellar tumor in children

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Astrocytoma is:
questions.explanation: Astrocytomas are tumors derived from astrocytes, classified as grade I (pilocytic, benign) to grade IV (glioblastoma, malignant). They are the most common primary brain tumors, typically in adults.
questions.keyConcept: Astrocytoma: glial tumor from astrocytes, grades I-IV

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Meningioma shows:
questions.explanation: Meningiomas are characterized by psammoma bodies (laminated calcified concretions), whorled patterns of spindle cells, and meningothelial cells. Rosenthal fibers are seen in pilocytic astrocytomas; vascular proliferation in glioblastomas.
questions.keyConcept: Meningioma characteristic: psammoma bodies, whorled pattern

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: A 9-year-old child has enlargement of the lateral ventricles with a 4 cm homogenous well-circumscribed mass within the 4th ventricle. Microscopically, it shows rosettes & pseudo-rosettes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Ependymomas arise from ependymal cells lining the ventricular system, especially common in children in the 4th ventricle. They show both rosettes (true ependymal rosettes) and pseudorosettes (perivascular).
questions.keyConcept: Ependymoma: rosettes and pseudorosettes, 4th ventricle in children

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Glioblastoma multiforme shows:
questions.explanation: Glioblastoma multiforme shows vascular proliferation (neovascularization with abnormal vessels), necrosis with pseudopalisading, and highly anaplastic cells. Rosenthal fibers are in pilocytic astrocytomas; rosette formation in medulloblastomas.
questions.keyConcept: Glioblastoma: vascular proliferation (not Rosenthal fibers or rosettes)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The following histological picture is not characteristic of Glioblastoma multiforme:
questions.explanation: Papillary formation is NOT characteristic of glioblastoma multiforme. GBM shows highly anaplastic cells, necrosis, tumor giant cells, and vascular proliferation. Papillary architecture is seen in papillary ependymomas or papillary meningiomas.
questions.keyConcept: Papillary formation is NOT characteristic of glioblastoma - EXCEPTION

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The most common brain tumor in children:
questions.explanation: Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumor in children, occurring in the cerebellum. It is a PNET (primitive neuroectodermal tumor) with small round blue cells.
questions.keyConcept: Medulloblastoma is most common malignant brain tumor in children

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The following is not a feature of meningioma:
questions.explanation: Meningiomas typically have a whorled cut surface (not whorly). The other statements about meningioma (adults, benign, psammoma bodies) are true. The question asks for what's NOT a feature.
questions.keyConcept: Meningioma has whorled pattern, not whorly surface - minor terminology

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which of the following tumors is malignant:
questions.explanation: Glioblastoma multiforme is a malignant brain tumor (WHO grade IV). Meningiomas and schwannomas are usually benign; neurofibromas are typically benign.
questions.keyConcept: Glioblastoma multiforme is the malignant tumor among the options

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: A male patient 40 years old presented with hemiplegia & deafness. Radiological examination showed a tumor at the cerebellopontine angle. Biopsy from this tumor showed a neurogenic tumor formed of hypercellular and hypocellular areas. The most possible diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Schwannomas (neurilemmomas) at the cerebellopontine angle show hypercellular (Antoni A) and hypocellular (Antoni B) areas. They arise from Schwann cells of vestibular portion of CN VIII.
questions.keyConcept: Schwannoma: Antoni A and B areas, hypercellular/hypocellular, cerebellopontine angle

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: An 18-year-old male presents with a well-circumscribed mass involving the 4th ventricle. Diagnostic microscopical findings in this condition include:
questions.explanation: Ependymomas show both rosettes (true ependymal) and pseudorosettes (perivascular). Rosenthal fibers are in pilocytic astrocytomas; Verocay bodies in schwannomas; chicken wire calcification in oligodendrogliomas.
questions.keyConcept: Ependymoma: rosettes and pseudorosettes (not Rosenthal fibers or Verocay bodies)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The following is not a type of glioma:
questions.explanation: Ganglioneuroma is a benign tumor of mature neurons (not a glioma). Astrocytomas, ependymomas, and glioblastomas are all gliomas (tumors of glial cells).
questions.keyConcept: Ganglioneuroma is NOT a glioma (it's a neuronal tumor) - EXCEPTION

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: A 33-year-old male presents with seizures, MRI shows an ill-defined area of infiltrative tumor expanding the frontal lobe. Biopsy of this lesion shows glial tissue with slightly increased cellularity and mild nuclear pleomorphism. No mitotic activity, no necrosis & no vascular proliferation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Grade II astrocytomas show increased cellularity, mild nuclear pleomorphism, but no mitotic activity, necrosis, or vascular proliferation. They are diffuse astrocytomas in young adults, slower growing than anaplastic or GBM.
questions.keyConcept: Grade II astrocytoma: slightly increased cellularity, mild pleomorphism, no necrosis/mitosis

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: A male patient 40 years presented with left-sided hemiplegia, brain MRI revealed a space-occupying lesion in the right cerebral hemisphere. Biopsy examination showed a highly cellular tumor with malignant cells, areas of necrosis & vascular proliferation. The most possible diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Glioblastoma multiforme shows highly cellular tumor with malignant cells, necrosis, and vascular proliferation. These features distinguish it from anaplastic astrocytoma (which lacks necrosis) and ependymoma.
questions.keyConcept: Glioblastoma: necrosis and vascular proliferation = hallmark features

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Oligodendroglioma is not a:
questions.explanation: Oligodendrogliomas are low-grade (grade II) tumors, not high-grade. They are glial tumors, cerebral tumors, and well-circumscribed. High-grade would be anaplastic oligodendroglioma (grade III).
questions.keyConcept: Oligodendroglioma is a low-grade tumor, NOT high-grade - EXCEPTION

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: A 9-year-old girl is evaluated for headache and ataxia over the last 2 months. A CT scan reveals a midline partially cystic cerebellar mass, microscopic examination shows elongated bipolar astrocytes with fibrillar processes and Rosenthal fibers. The diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Pilocytic astrocytoma (WHO grade I) shows elongated bipolar astrocytes with Rosenthal fibers and fibrillar processes. It is benign, cystic, midline cerebellar tumor in children with good prognosis.
