questions.keyConcept: Pilocytic astrocytoma: Rosenthal fibers, bipolar astrocytes, cystic cerebellar tumor

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The following tumor arises from the lining of the ventricular system:
questions.explanation: Ependymomas arise from ependymal cells that line the ventricular system and central canal of the spinal cord. They can occur throughout the neuraxis, commonly in the 4th ventricle.
questions.keyConcept: Ependymoma arises from ependymal lining of ventricular system

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Astrocytoma is a:
questions.explanation: Astrocytomas are glial tumors derived from astrocytes, the most common primary brain tumors. They range from grade I (pilocytic, benign) to grade IV (glioblastoma, highly malignant).
questions.keyConcept: Astrocytoma is a glial tumor (from astrocytes)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Oligodendrogliomas are not characterized by:
questions.explanation: Oligodendrogliomas do NOT typically show activation of the MAPK pathway. They characteristically have IDH1/IDH2 mutations and 1p/19q codeletion. MAPK activation is seen in pilocytic astrocytomas (BRAF fusion).
questions.keyConcept: Oligodendroglioma: IDH mutation, 1p/19q codeletion (NOT MAPK activation) - EXCEPTION
options: Activation of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is true about meningococcal meningitis?
questions.explanation: Meningococcal meningitis primarily affects young adults (not elderly), involves the leptomeninges (pia-arachnoid), not primarily the dura. Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome (acute adrenal insufficiency) is a serious complication due to bilateral adrenal hemorrhage.
questions.keyConcept: Meningococcal meningitis: young adults, leptomeninges, Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome
options: It most commonly affects adults around the sixth decade of life.
The dura mater is mainly affected by suppuration.
The condition may be complicated by acute adrenal insufficiency.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Rabies is transmitted to CNS via:
questions.explanation: Rabies virus travels from the bite site via retrograde axonal transport through peripheral nerves to the CNS. This is why post-exposure prophylaxis must be administered promptly before the virus reaches the CNS.
questions.keyConcept: Rabies spreads to CNS via retrograde axonal transport through peripheral nerves

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A child with tuberculous meningitis, his CSF examination will show an increased number of:
questions.explanation: Tuberculous meningitis causes lymphocytic pleocytosis in CSF (typically 100-500 cells/ microliter). Neutrophils are seen in acute bacterial meningitis; macrophages and plasma cells may be present but lymphocytes predominate.
questions.keyConcept: TB meningitis: lymphocytic pleocytosis in CSF

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Muscle paralysis in case of poliomyelitis is due to:
questions.explanation: Poliovirus selectively destroys anterior horn cells (lower motor neurons) in the spinal cord, causing flaccid paralysis. The muscle paralysis is NOT due to direct viral damage to muscle or toxin production.
questions.keyConcept: Polio paralysis from destruction of anterior horn motor neurons in spinal cord
options: Destruction of the muscle fibers by the toxins of the organisms.
Inflammation of the nerves supplying the affected muscles.
Degeneration of their anterior horn cells in the spinal cord.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Poliomyelitis is a:
questions.explanation: Poliomyelitis is caused by poliovirus, an enterovirus (RNA virus). It is transmitted fecal- orally and causes anterior horn cell destruction leading to flaccid paralysis.
questions.keyConcept: Poliomyelitis is a viral infection (poliovirus, enterovirus)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The cause of death in rabies is:
questions.explanation: Death in rabies is due to respiratory muscle paralysis (bulbar palsy affecting respiratory muscles), not heart failure or direct respiratory center failure. The virus destroys motor neurons in the brainstem.
questions.keyConcept: Rabies death from respiratory muscle paralysis (bulbar palsy)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Infection spreads from suppurative lung diseases to the brain via:
questions.explanation: Infection spreads from suppurative lung diseases (lung abscess, bronchiectasis) to the brain via vertebral veins (Batson's venous plexus), which connects the pelvic veins to the intracranial venous sinuses.
questions.keyConcept: Lung infection spreads to brain via vertebral veins (Batson's plexus)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Rabies is a:
questions.explanation: Rabies is caused by the rabies virus (Lyssavirus, Rhabdoviridae family). It is transmitted through animal bites via retrograde axonal transport to the CNS.
questions.keyConcept: Rabies is a viral infection (rabies virus, Rhabdoviridae)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Myotic cerebral aneurysms are due to:
questions.explanation: Mycotic (septic) aneurysms result from septic emboli lodging in cerebral vessels, typically from subacute bacterial endocarditis. The emboli cause arterial wall weakening and aneurysm formation.
questions.keyConcept: Mycotic aneurysms from septic emboli of subacute bacterial endocarditis
options: Congenital weakness of the wall of cerebral vessels.
Septic emboli from subacute bacterial endocarditis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Subarachnoid hemorrhage is due to:
questions.explanation: Subarachnoid hemorrhage can result from trauma, rupture of congenital berry aneurysms, or vasculitis (inflammation of Circle of Willis vessels). All options are correct causes.
questions.keyConcept: SAH: trauma, berry aneurysm rupture, or vasculitis (all of the above)
options: Inflammation of the vessels of the circle of Willis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 58-year-old hypertensive patient presents with sudden onset of hemiplegia followed by symptoms of increased intracranial tension (headache & vomiting). A CT scan shows extensive intracerebral hemorrhage in the region of basal ganglia. The most probable diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms are small aneurysms that form on small penetrating arteries in hypertensive patients, most commonly affecting the basal ganglia (lenticulostriate arteries) and causing hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage.
questions.keyConcept: Hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage: Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms in basal ganglia

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following antiepileptic drugs is not an enzyme inducer?
questions.explanation: Valproate is not a CYP enzyme inducer; it actually inhibits some cytochrome P450 enzymes. Phenytoin, carbamazepine, and phenobarbital are all enzyme inducers that increase metabolism of other drugs.
questions.keyConcept: Valproate is NOT an enzyme inducer (unlike phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is a wrong statement regarding antiepileptic drugs?
questions.explanation: Pregnant women with epilepsy should NOT discontinue antiepileptic drugs abruptly - the risk of seizures may outweigh the risks of the medication. Treatment should be continued with the lowest effective dose of the safest drug.
questions.keyConcept: Pregnant women should NOT discontinue AEDs abruptly (risky to mother and fetus) - FALSE
options: Females who get pregnant should discontinue the antiepileptic drug
They are contraindicated in neuropathic pain
Carbamazepine antagonizes the action of antidiuretic hormone

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following anesthetic agents is not acting through increase GABA activity?
questions.explanation: Ketamine acts as an NMDA receptor antagonist, not through GABA enhancement. Halothane, propofol, and isoflurane all enhance GABA-A receptor activity (inhibitory neurotransmitter).
questions.keyConcept: Ketamine acts on NMDA receptors, not through GABA enhancement

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is 1st choice as empiric antibiotic in meningitis suspected to streptococcal agalactia in 55 year old patient?
questions.explanation: For meningitis suspected of Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Strep) in a 55-year-old, vancomycin (for resistant pneumococcus) plus ceftriaxone is empiric coverage. Ampicillin is added for Listeria in elderly, but the primary coverage is vancomycin + ceftriaxone.
questions.keyConcept: Empiric meningitis coverage in elderly: Vancomycin + ceftriaxone (for resistant Strep)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is correct regarding Fingolimod?
questions.explanation: Fingolimod prevents T lymphocyte migration from lymph nodes by blocking S1P receptors, decreases BBB invasion by trapping T cells in lymph nodes, and should be used cautiously in cardiac patients (first-dose bradycardia).
questions.keyConcept: Fingolimod: traps T cells in lymph nodes, caution in cardiac patients
options: Decrease BBB invasion by T- lymphocyte
Prevent T lymphocyte migration from lymph node
Used with caution in cardiac patients

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A drug effective in reducing emotional bluntness in schizophrenics is:
questions.explanation: Clozapine (atypical antipsychotic) is effective for treating negative symptoms of schizophrenia including emotional bluntness and social withdrawal. It has affinity for multiple receptors including dopamine and serotonin.
questions.keyConcept: Clozapine reduces negative symptoms (emotional bluntness) in schizophrenia

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following opioid drug should be avoided in patient taking MAOI:
questions.explanation: Meperidine (pethidine) should be avoided with MAOIs due to risk of serotonin syndrome and severe adverse reactions. It has serotonergic properties unlike other opioids. Morphine, fentanyl, and codeine do not have this specific interaction.
questions.keyConcept: Meperidine contraindicated with MAOIs (serotonin syndrome risk)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Lidocaine is preferred to bupivacaine in local anesthesia due to:
questions.explanation: Lidocaine has faster onset (lower pKa means more rapid crossing of nerve membrane) compared to bupivacaine. Bupivacaine has longer duration and higher potency but slower onset.
questions.keyConcept: Lidocaine preferred over bupivacaine due to more rapid onset (lower pKa)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Ethosuximide is useful in:
questions.explanation: Ethosuximide is the first-line treatment for absence seizures (petit mal) by blocking T-type calcium channels in thalamic neurons. It is not effective for partial epilepsy or tonic-clonic seizures.
questions.keyConcept: Ethosuximide: first-line for absence seizures (not partial or tonic-clonic)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following antiepileptic drug is not preferred in pregnancy:
questions.explanation: Valproate is teratogenic (neural tube defects) and should be avoided in pregnancy. Lamotrigine and carbamazepine are safer options but still require careful risk-benefit analysis. All AEDs have some risk.
questions.keyConcept: Valproate is most teratogenic AED, not preferred in pregnancy

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following anesthetic agent is not acting through increase GABA activity:
questions.explanation: Ketamine acts as an NMDA receptor antagonist, not through GABA enhancement. Halothane, propofol, and isoflurane all enhance GABA-A receptor activity.
questions.keyConcept: Ketamine acts on NMDA receptors, not through GABA enhancement (duplicate of 334)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is not correctly matched to its mechanism of action?
questions.explanation: Valproate's mechanism involves multiple mechanisms: inhibiting GABA transaminase, but also blocking sodium channels and increasing GABA synthesis. The statement as written is oversimplified but not entirely incorrect. However, ethosuximide does block T-type Ca++ channels; clonazepam potentiates GABA, not Cl channel blockade per se.
questions.keyConcept: Valproate: multiple mechanisms including GABA transaminase inhibition (partial correct)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Riluzole is prescribed in Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis to:
questions.explanation: Riluzole is a glutamate release inhibitor that modestly prolongs survival in ALS (about 2-3 months) by decreasing the need for ventilator support. It does not significantly decrease dementia onset or headache/confusion.
questions.keyConcept: Riluzole in ALS: decreases need for ventilator, modestly prolongs survival

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Nicotine abuse may be managed by:
questions.explanation: Nicotine dependence can be managed with varenicline (partial nicotinic agonist) or bupropion (norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor). Buprenorphine is for opioid dependence; acamprosate is for alcohol dependence.
questions.keyConcept: Nicotine cessation: varenicline and bupropion (not buprenorphine or acamprosate)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following analgesic is not recommended to be taken in renal failure or more than 48 hours for fear of convulsions:
questions.explanation: Meperidine (pethidine) should be avoided in renal failure and not used for more than 48 hours due to accumulation of normeperidine, which causes seizures. Morphine, codeine, and tramadol are safer alternatives.
questions.keyConcept: Meperidine contraindicated in renal failure (normeperidine accumulation causes seizures)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following is not true about local anesthetics:
questions.explanation: Bupivacaine is LONG-acting (not short-acting), providing 2-4 hours of anesthesia. Lidocaine is an intermediate-acting amide. Adding bicarbonate speeds onset; benzocaine is used for topical anesthesia.
questions.keyConcept: Bupivacaine is LONG-acting local anesthetic (not short-acting) - FALSE
options: Adding sodium bicarbonate increases activity of local anesthetics
Benzocaine is used as surface anesthetic

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following antiepileptic drug is not an enzyme inducer:
questions.explanation: Valproate is not a CYP enzyme inducer; it actually inhibits some cytochrome P450 enzymes. Phenytoin, carbamazepine, and phenobarbital are all potent enzyme inducers.
questions.keyConcept: Valproate NOT an enzyme inducer (inhibits CYP enzymes)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following anesthetic agent is not acting through increase GABA activity:
questions.explanation: Ketamine acts as an NMDA receptor antagonist, producing dissociative anesthesia. Halothane, propofol, and isoflurane all enhance GABA-A receptor activity.
questions.keyConcept: Ketamine: NMDA receptor antagonist (not GABA enhancement)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is 1st choice as empiric antibiotic in meningitis suspected to streptococcal agalactia in 55 year old patient?
questions.explanation: For meningitis in patients over 50, vancomycin + ceftriaxone is the empiric regimen to cover resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae and other pathogens. Ampicillin is added for Listeria monocytogenes in this age group.
questions.keyConcept: Empiric meningitis coverage in elderly: vancomycin + ceftriaxone

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is correct regarding Fingolimod?
questions.explanation: Fingolimod is a sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor modulator that prevents T cell egress from lymph nodes, reducing CNS infiltration. First-dose cardiac monitoring is required due to bradycardia risk.
questions.keyConcept: Fingolimod: S1P modulator, traps T cells in lymph nodes, cardiac caution needed
options: Decrease BBB invasion by T- lymphocyte
Prevent T lymphocyte migration from lymph node
Used with caution in cardiac patients

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A drug effective in reducing emotional bluntness in schizophrenics is:
questions.explanation: Clozapine is most effective for negative symptoms of schizophrenia (emotional bluntness, avolition) due to its unique receptor profile including dopamine D4 and serotonin 5-HT2A antagonism.
questions.keyConcept: Clozapine effective for negative symptoms (emotional bluntness) in schizophrenia

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following opioid drug should be avoided in patient taking MAOI:
questions.explanation: Meperidine (pethidine) is absolutely contraindicated with MAOIs due to risk of serotonin syndrome and severe hypotensive/hypertensive crises. This is a classic drug interaction tested frequently.
questions.keyConcept: Meperidine contraindicated with MAOIs (serotonin syndrome risk)
